conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.front: What is advance care planning, and why does it matter?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.back: The process by which a person with capacity records their wishes for future care/treatment, so that if they later lose capacity their voice still guides decisions. It sits at the meeting of medical law and end-of-life practice.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.front: Which statute underpins advance care planning and adult consent in England & Wales?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.back: The Mental Capacity Act 2005. An advance document only becomes relevant once capacity for that specific decision is lost.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.front: List the 5 statutory principles of the Mental Capacity Act 2005.
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.back:
• (1) Presume capacity unless established otherwise.
  • (2) Support the person to decide (all practicable help) before deeming them unable.
  • (3) An unwise decision does not equal lack of capacity.
  • (4) Act in the person's best interests if they lack capacity.
  • (5) Choose the least restrictive option.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.front: Describe the 2-stage capacity test.
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.back:
• Stage 1: is there an impairment of, or disturbance in, the mind/brain?
  • Stage 2: does it mean the person cannot understand, retain, use/weigh, or communicate the decision?
Capacity is decision-specific and time-specific.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.front: Does an unwise decision indicate a lack of capacity?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.back: No. A capacitous adult can refuse any treatment (even life-saving) for any or no reason — an unwise choice is not incapacity (e.g. a Jehovah's Witness refusing blood).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.front: What is the hierarchy of end-of-life documents by legal force?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.back:
• 1. Advance Decision to Refuse Treatment — legally binding if valid and applicable.
  • 2. Lasting Power of Attorney — appoints a decision-maker.
  • 3. Advance statement — influential but not binding.
The top two rungs are ordered by date, not by type: between an ADRT and an LPA covering the same treatment, the later document prevails.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.front: What is an Advance Decision to Refuse Treatment (ADRT)?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.back: A 'living will' — lets an adult refuse specified treatments in advance, to apply if they later lose capacity. A valid and applicable ADRT is legally binding — the same force as a contemporaneous refusal by a competent patient; overriding it risks battery/liability.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.front: What can an ADRT NOT do?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.back:
• It can only refuse treatment, never demand it, and never anything unlawful — euthanasia is murder and assisting suicide is a separate criminal offence.
  • It cannot refuse basic care (warmth, shelter, hygiene, and the offer of food and drink by mouth), but it CAN refuse clinically assisted nutrition and hydration, which is medical treatment.
  • It also cannot refuse treatment for a mental disorder given under the Mental Health Act 1983 to a detained patient.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.front: What makes an ADRT valid and applicable?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.back:
• Valid — made at 18+ by someone with capacity to make it; not withdrawn while they had capacity; they have not since created an LPA covering the same treatment; and they have done nothing clearly inconsistent with it remaining their fixed decision.
  • Applicable — they now lack capacity for that decision; the treatment is the one specified; any stated circumstances are present; and there are no reasonable grounds to believe circumstances have arisen that they did not anticipate and that would have changed their decision.
It binds you only if both are met.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.front: What extra formalities are required for an ADRT to refuse LIFE-SUSTAINING treatment?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.back: It must be in writing, signed, and witnessed, and explicitly state it applies 'even if life is at risk' (the single most-tested detail). If these aren't met it is not binding, but still counts as evidence of wishes.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.front: What is a Lasting Power of Attorney (LPA), and what are the two types?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.back: The donor appoints an attorney to make decisions if they lose capacity. Two types: Health & Welfare and Property & Financial Affairs.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.front: Which LPA covers medical treatment, and what are the key conditions?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.back: Only the Health & Welfare LPA covers medical treatment, and only once the donor lacks capacity. It covers life-sustaining treatment only if expressly stated, and must be registered with the Office of the Public Guardian.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.front: What are the limits on an attorney's power under a Health & Welfare LPA?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.back: The attorney must act in the donor's best interests — they cannot demand treatment clinicians judge inappropriate, and cannot consent to something a valid later ADRT has already refused.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.front: What is an advance statement, and what is its legal weight?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.back: A written/verbal statement of wishes, preferences, values and beliefs (e.g. 'I'd prefer to die at home'). It is NOT legally binding, but must be taken into account in any best-interests decision.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.front: State the 'later document wins' interaction rule.
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.back: Between an ADRT and an LPA for the same treatment, the later document takes precedence: an LPA made after an ADRT can override it; an ADRT made after an LPA overrides the attorney.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.front: What does a valid, applicable ADRT override?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.back: A valid, applicable ADRT overrides best-interests decision-making, and the Court of Protection cannot overrule it — the court can only declare whether it exists and whether it is valid and applicable. The safety valve: while that is genuinely in dispute and a decision is being sought from the court, clinicians may lawfully give life-sustaining treatment to prevent death or serious deterioration.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.front: What is the order of authority when a patient lacks capacity?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.back:
• A Health & Welfare LPA attorney can consent to or refuse treatment once the donor lacks capacity — but can refuse life-sustaining treatment only if the LPA expressly says so.
  • A court-appointed welfare deputy is rarely appointed and can never refuse consent to life-sustaining treatment.
Neither can demand treatment the team judges inappropriate.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.front: Can family / next-of-kin consent to or refuse treatment for an adult who lacks capacity?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.back: No — unless they hold a Health & Welfare LPA (or are a court-appointed deputy). Family are consulted and their account is evidence of wishes, but they cannot themselves consent or refuse.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.front: What is a DNACPR decision, and what does it cover?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.back: 'Do Not Attempt CPR' — a clinical decision recorded in the notes that CPR should not be attempted if the heart/breathing stops. It is specific to CPR only and does not affect any other treatment.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.front: Who must be involved in a DNACPR decision?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.back:
• Whether CPR is offered is a clinical decision — a patient cannot demand CPR that would not work.
  • But a capacitous patient can refuse it, and a valid, applicable ADRT refusing CPR is binding.
  • There is a legal duty to inform and involve the patient (or those close to them if they lack capacity) unless doing so would cause the patient physical or psychological harm — distress alone is not enough.
  • A DNACPR must never rest on age, frailty or disability alone (CQC), is reviewable and revocable, and a second opinion should be offered if there is disagreement.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.front: What is ReSPECT, and is it legally binding?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.back: Recommended Summary Plan for Emergency Care and Treatment — a broader emergency care plan recording recommendations for CPR and the wider ceiling of treatment (admission, ICU, ventilation). It is a recommendation/summary, NOT itself legally binding (unlike an ADRT), and increasingly replaces standalone DNACPR forms.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.front: When must an Independent Mental Capacity Advocate (IMCA) be appointed?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.back:
• When a person lacks capacity
  • has no one else to consult (no family/friends, LPA or deputy)
  • and a serious decision is needed (serious medical treatment or a change of accommodation).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.front: What is benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV)?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.back: Recurrent, brief episodes of vertigo triggered by head movement, caused by displaced otoconia (calcium-carbonate crystals) in the semicircular canals. It is the single commonest cause of vertigo and a major contributor to falls in the elderly.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.front: Explain the pathophysiology of BPPV.
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.back: Otoconia normally sit in the utricle; in BPPV they dislodge into a semicircular canal (most often the posterior canal, ~85–90%). Head movement makes the loose crystals move the endolymph abnormally, giving the brain a false signal of rotation → vertigo + nystagmus. This is canalithiasis.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.front: What is the diagnostic triad of BPPV?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.back:
• Positional trigger
  • very short duration (usually under 30 seconds, always under a minute)
  • NO hearing loss or tinnitus.
This triad separates BPPV from Meniere's (hearing loss/tinnitus) and vestibular neuronitis (constant/prolonged), and from central causes.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.front: List the causes/associations of BPPV.
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.back:
• Usually idiopathic
  • also head trauma
  • ageing
  • prolonged bed rest
  • and following vestibular neuronitis/labyrinthitis.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.front: What are the classic triggers and duration of BPPV episodes?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.back:
Triggered by head movements — classically
  • rolling over in bed
  • lying down
  • looking up ('top-shelf vertigo')
  • bending forward.
Each episode is very brief (usually under 30 seconds, always under a minute) and settles if the head is kept still; the patient is well between episodes. In older people the presentation is often atypical — vague unsteadiness or unexplained falls rather than clear spinning.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.front: Which single feature best distinguishes BPPV from Meniere's disease and labyrinthitis?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.back: The absence of hearing loss and tinnitus. Meniere's has vertigo + hearing loss + tinnitus + aural fullness; labyrinthitis has vertigo + hearing loss (post-viral).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.front: What is the gold-standard diagnostic test for (posterior canal) BPPV, and how is it performed?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.back:
The Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre ('D for Diagnosis'):
  • patient sits with head turned 45deg toward the side tested
  • rapidly lie them back with the head hanging ~20–30deg below the couch edge
  • hold and watch the eyes for ~30–60s.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.front: What constitutes a positive Dix-Hallpike test?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.back: After a brief latency (a few seconds), upbeating torsional nystagmus with the upper pole beating toward the affected (lower) ear, lasting under a minute, plus reproduction of the patient's vertigo; it is fatigable on repeat. Latency, transience and fatigability all point away from a central cause. A negative test does not exclude BPPV — repeat it and test the other side.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.front: Which test is used to diagnose horizontal (lateral) canal BPPV?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.back: The supine roll test (not Dix-Hallpike). Horizontal-canal BPPV is less common than posterior-canal BPPV.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.front: Is imaging needed to diagnose BPPV?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.back: No — no imaging is needed for typical BPPV. Reserve MRI for atypical features or central red flags.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.front: What is the first-line treatment for posterior-canal BPPV?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.back: The Epley manoeuvre ('E for treatment') — a canalith repositioning procedure that rolls the otoconia out of the posterior canal back into the utricle. Highly effective: over 90% are symptom-free, usually within one or two sessions. The Semont manoeuvre is an equally acceptable alternative; horizontal-canal BPPV needs a barbecue (Lempert) roll instead. No postural restrictions are needed afterwards.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.front: What are Brandt-Daroff exercises, and how do they compare to Epley?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.back: Patient-performed home exercises — an option if Epley is unavailable/untolerated or for residual symptoms. They are less effective than the Epley manoeuvre.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.front: Why are vestibular sedatives NOT the treatment for BPPV?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.back:
Vestibular sedatives (prochlorperazine, cinnarizine, cyclizine) have no useful role — each attack is over in under a minute, so there is nothing to suppress; they do not treat the mechanical cause and they delay central compensation. In older people they are actively harmful:
  • sedation
  • postural hypotension
  • confusion
  • increased falls risk
  • and with prochlorperazine drug-induced parkinsonism and tardive dyskinesia.
Betahistine is a histamine analogue used in Meniere's, not an antihistamine and not a BPPV treatment. (Short-term prochlorperazine IS appropriate in acute vestibular neuronitis.)

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.front: What is the natural course of BPPV?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.back: Self-limiting — most cases resolve within weeks to ~6 months even untreated, but repositioning (Epley) speeds resolution dramatically. Recurrence is common (~50% over years).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.front: What safety advice should you give a patient with BPPV, especially if elderly?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.back: Counsel on falls risk and occupational hazards (ladders, heights, machinery), and advise not to drive while symptomatic. The DVLA must be told about liability to sudden, unprovoked disabling giddiness — BPPV is provoked and positional, so a controlled Group 1 driver usually need not notify, but Group 2 (bus/lorry) rules are stricter. BPPV is a major, curable contributor to falls in older people.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.front: List the central red flags that should prompt urgent imaging/stroke pathway in a patient with vertigo.
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.back:
• Vertical or direction-changing nystagmus
  • other neurological signs (ataxia, diplopia, dysarthria, limb/CN signs)
  • inability to stand/walk
  • severe headache
  • and sudden persistent vertigo
— think posterior-circulation stroke.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.front: How does the nystagmus of BPPV differ from that of a central cause?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.back:
• BPPV (posterior canal): upbeating and torsional, with the upper pole of the eye beating toward the undermost (affected) ear; short latency of a few seconds, transient (settles within a minute) and fatigable on repeat testing.
  • Central: vertical (especially downbeat), direction-changing or purely torsional, with no latency, non-fatiguing and persistent, often with other neurological signs.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.front: When should a patient with suspected BPPV be referred to ENT / a balance clinic?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.back:
• If the diagnosis is uncertain
  • there are atypical or central features
  • symptoms persist despite repeated repositioning (in practice beyond about 4 weeks)
  • or there is frequent recurrence.
Surgery (posterior-canal occlusion) is a last resort for intractable cases.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.front: Give the key differentials for BPPV and their distinguishing features.
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.back:
• Meniere's — vertigo + hearing loss + tinnitus + aural fullness.
  • Vestibular neuronitis — constant, prolonged, post-viral, NO hearing loss.
  • Labyrinthitis — like neuronitis but WITH hearing loss.
  • Vestibular migraine — recurrent vertigo lasting minutes to hours with migrainous features and a migraine history, no hearing loss.
  • Central (stroke/tumour/MS) — neuro signs, abnormal nystagmus.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.front: What does the HINTS examination help distinguish?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.back: It helps differentiate a peripheral cause of acute vestibular syndrome from a central (e.g. posterior-circulation stroke) cause at the bedside (Head Impulse, Nystagmus, Test of Skew).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.front: What is comprehensive geriatric assessment (CGA)?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.back: A multidimensional, multidisciplinary diagnostic and therapeutic process that assesses an older person's medical, functional, psychological, and social capabilities and problems, to build a coordinated, integrated plan for treatment and follow-up.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.front: What are the two defining pillars of CGA?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.back: It is multidimensional (assesses several domains, not just the presenting complaint) and multidisciplinary (delivered by a team, not one doctor). Remember: holistic + team-based + iterative plan.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.front: Is CGA a questionnaire or a score?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.back: Neither — CGA is a process. Its output is a problem list and a coordinated, patient-centred management plan that is revisited iteratively.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.front: Why does CGA exist / what problem does it solve?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.back: Older people with frailty and multimorbidity don't fit the 'one patient, one diagnosis' model. A standard disease-focused clerking misses the falls, cognition, polypharmacy, and isolation — CGA catches all of these at once.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.front: What is the key outcome evidence for CGA?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.back: Older people with moderate-severe frailty admitted as an emergency who receive CGA are more likely to be alive and living in their own home at follow-up, and less likely to be institutionalised. Mortality is largely unchanged, and effects on length of stay and readmission are inconsistent — the living-at-home outcome is the one to quote.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.front: What are the domains of CGA?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.back: Classically four — medical, functional, psychological, social. The British Geriatrics Society framework expands this to six: physical/medical, psychological, functional, social, environmental and future wishes.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.front: What does the PHYSICAL/medical domain of CGA cover?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.back:
• Comorbidities/multimorbidity
  • frailty syndromes (falls, immobility, incontinence, delirium)
  • medication review/polypharmacy
  • continence
  • nutrition
  • pain
  • and sensory (vision/hearing) and skin.
Tools: problem list, STOPP/START, bloods, MUST (nutrition).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.front: What does the PSYCHOLOGICAL domain cover, and which tools are used?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.back: Cognition (dementia, delirium) and mood (depression, anxiety), plus mental capacity. Tools: AMTS or a brief screen such as 6CIT, with MoCA where more detail is needed; 4AT for delirium; Geriatric Depression Scale for mood.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.front: What does the FUNCTIONAL domain cover, and which tools are used?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.back:
• Basic ADLs and instrumental ADLs (IADLs)
  • mobility
  • balance
  • and gait.
Tools: Barthel Index (ADLs) and the Timed Up-and-Go test.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.front: Distinguish basic ADLs from instrumental ADLs (IADLs).
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.back:
• Basic ADLs = self-care: washing, dressing, feeding, toileting, transfers.
  • IADLs = more complex independent-living tasks: cooking, shopping, managing finances, managing medications, using transport.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.front: What do the SOCIAL and ENVIRONMENTAL domains cover?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.back:
• Social: care/support network, informal carers (and carer strain), formal care package, finances, safeguarding.
  • Environmental: home setup, falls hazards, aids/adaptations, access — assessed by an occupational-therapy home assessment.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.front: What does the FUTURE WISHES domain of CGA cover?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.back:
• Advance care planning
  • ADRT/LPA
  • ceilings of treatment
  • ReSPECT/DNACPR
  • and preferred place of care.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.front: Who are the core members of the CGA multidisciplinary team?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.back: Geriatrician/medical lead, nurses, physiotherapist (mobility/balance/falls), occupational therapist (function/ADLs/home assessment), pharmacist (polypharmacy review), dietitian, SALT, and social worker — with the patient and family/carers at the centre.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.front: Which team member primarily assesses ADLs, home environment, and aids/adaptations?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.back: The occupational therapist (OT).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.front: Who usually carries out the structured medication review in CGA, and who makes the final deprescribing decision?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.back:
• The pharmacist carries out the structured medication review (using STOPP/START)
  • deprescribing decisions are made by the responsible prescriber — geriatrician or GP — together with the patient.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.front: Outline the five steps of the CGA process.
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.back:
• (1) Identify the right patients — a frailty screen (Clinical Frailty Scale, PRISMA-7, gait speed); in practice CFS 5 or more triggers a frailty pathway and CGA, and in primary care frailty is case-found with the electronic Frailty Index.
  • (2) Multidimensional assessment across domains.
  • (3) MDT meeting to synthesise a shared problem list.
  • (4) Coordinated management plan with patient-centred goals.
  • (5) Implement, review and iterate with defined follow-up.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.front: Which patients should CGA be targeted at?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.back: Older people with frailty and multimorbidity — those who benefit most — identified with a frailty tool (Clinical Frailty Scale, PRISMA-7, gait speed). Not every older patient.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.front: In which settings is CGA delivered, and where is the evidence strongest?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.back:
• Acute 'front-door' frailty units / ED / Same Day Emergency Care
  • inpatient geriatric wards (strongest evidence)
  • community and home-based
  • perioperative (POPS — proactive care of older people undergoing surgery)
  • and oncology (fitness for treatment).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.front: What are the 'geriatric giants' / frailty syndromes that CGA is designed to surface?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.back: Falls, immobility, delirium/confusion, incontinence, and iatrogenic harm (polypharmacy) — the syndromes a disease-focused clerking tends to miss.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.front: What is deconditioning, and how does CGA address it?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.back: The harm of unnecessary bed rest (loss of muscle strength and function). Urgent/front-door CGA aims to prevent unnecessary admission and deconditioning and to promote early mobilisation.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: What is delirium?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back: An acute, fluctuating disturbance of consciousness, attention, cognition, and perception (an acute confusional state) that develops over hours to days and is caused by an underlying physical trigger.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: Why does delirium matter clinically?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back: It is a 'geriatric giant', very common in unwell older inpatients, a marker of serious illness (roughly doubles mortality, predicts future dementia and institutionalisation), and is often reversible if the cause is found and treated — yet it is massively under-recognised (especially the hypoactive form).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: Delirium is a symptom, not a diagnosis — what does this mean for management?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back: Delirium is a 'flashing light' signalling an acute physical problem. You must always find and treat the underlying cause; the management is treat the cause + supportive/environmental care, with drugs a reluctant last resort.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: What is the hallmark cognitive feature of delirium?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back: Inattention (markedly impaired attention) — the defining feature, alongside acute onset and a fluctuating course.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: Contrast delirium with dementia (onset, course, consciousness, attention, reversibility).
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back:
• Delirium: acute onset (hours-days), fluctuating course (worse at night), impaired/altered consciousness, markedly impaired attention, usually reversible.
  • Dementia: insidious (months-years), stable/slowly progressive, normal consciousness (until late), attention relatively preserved early, irreversible.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: How do hallucinations differ between delirium and dementia?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back: Hallucinations (often visual) are common in delirium; they are less common in dementia — except dementia with Lewy bodies, where visual hallucinations are characteristic.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: If you cannot tell whether a patient has delirium, dementia, or delirium-on-dementia, what should you do?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back: Treat the delirium first (NICE). Obtain a collateral history to establish the cognitive baseline.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: Name the three motor subtypes of delirium.
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back:
• Hyperactive (agitated, restless, aggressive, hallucinating, wandering)
  • Hypoactive (withdrawn, quiet, drowsy, slow)
  • and Mixed (fluctuates between the two).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: Which motor subtype of delirium is the commonest and most dangerous, and why?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back: Hypoactive delirium — it is the commonest and most dangerous because it is missed (mistaken for depression, fatigue, or 'just dementia') and carries worse outcomes. Actively look for it.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: List predisposing risk factors for delirium.
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back:
• Older age
  • pre-existing dementia/cognitive impairment
  • frailty
  • sensory impairment (poor vision/hearing)
  • previous delirium
  • multimorbidity
  • and polypharmacy.
NICE defines being 'at risk' by four factors to assess at presentation: age 65 or over; cognitive impairment or dementia; current hip fracture; severe illness.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: List precipitating risk factors for delirium.
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back:
• Acute illness/infection
  • surgery (especially hip fracture)
  • new drugs
  • dehydration
  • pain
  • catheterisation
  • and change of environment.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: What does the 'PINCH ME' mnemonic for delirium causes stand for?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back:
• Pain
  • Infection (UTI, pneumonia, sepsis)
  • Nutrition/poor intake
  • Constipation (and urinary retention)
  • Hydration (dehydration)
  • Medication (opioids, anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, steroids; and withdrawal) & Metabolic
  • Environment & Electrolytes.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: Which are the 'big two' groups of delirium causes to always consider?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back:
• Infection (UTI, pneumonia, sepsis)
  • and drugs/medication (including new drugs and withdrawal).
Also think metabolic disturbance, constipation/retention, and intracranial causes.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: Which medications are commonly deliriogenic?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back: Opioids, anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, and steroids; also withdrawal from alcohol or benzodiazepines. A medication review is a core part of assessment.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: What is the recommended UK screening tool for delirium, and its components?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back:
The 4AT (NICE):
  • (1) Alertness
  • (2) AMT-4 (age, date of birth, place, year)
  • (3) Attention — months of the year backwards
  • (4) Acute change/fluctuation.
≥4 suggests possible delirium ± cognitive impairment; 1–3 suggests possible cognitive impairment; 0 makes delirium unlikely.Delirium fluctuates, so repeat the screen if suspicion persists.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: Which delirium screening tool is used in critical care/ICU?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back: The CAM-ICU — or the ICDSC — rather than the 4AT, in critical care and in the recovery room after surgery (NICE).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: What investigations help find the cause of delirium?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back:
• Observations/sepsis screen and saturations
  • an immediate bedside capillary glucose
  • bloods (FBC, U&E, calcium, glucose, LFTs, TFTs, CRP, magnesium)
  • urinalysis/culture (cautiously)
  • a bladder scan for retention
  • CXR
  • ECG
  • medication review
  • and CT head if focal signs, head injury, or no cause is found.
Take a collateral history for baseline.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: Why must you be cautious about diagnosing a UTI as the cause of delirium in an older person?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is common in the elderly — a positive urine dip alone does not prove a UTI is the cause. Don't anchor on it; keep looking for other precipitants (per PINCH ME).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: What is the definitive treatment of delirium?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back:
Treat the underlying cause(s) — e.g.
  • antibiotics for infection
  • analgesia for pain
  • rehydration
  • relieve constipation/retention
  • stop the culprit drug
  • correct electrolytes.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: What is the first-line management of the delirium itself (before any drugs)?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back:
Non-pharmacological/supportive care:
  • reorientation (clocks, calendars, familiar objects, staff introductions)
  • involve family/carers
  • optimise environment (lighting, quiet, normal sleep-wake cycle)
  • sensory aids (glasses/hearing aids)
  • mobilise
  • hydrate
  • attend to nutrition and bowels/bladder
  • avoid catheters/lines
  • manage pain
  • and verbal/non-verbal de-escalation.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: When and how should medication be used in delirium?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back: Last resort only — if the patient is distressed or a risk to themselves/others AND de-escalation has failed. Use short-term, lowest-dose haloperidol (usually ≤1 week), typically 500 micrograms to start in an older person, staying well below the BNF maximum of 5 mg in 24 hours. Do a baseline ECG and correct electrolytes first (MHRA) — haloperidol prolongs the QTc — and remember antipsychotics also raise stroke and death in older people with dementia (MHRA). Review daily.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: In which patients must you AVOID antipsychotics (haloperidol) for delirium, and what is used instead?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back: Parkinson's disease and dementia with Lewy bodies — haloperidol is contraindicated (MHRA), a hard contraindication rather than a caution, because it causes severe and sometimes life-threatening extrapyramidal reactions. Use a benzodiazepine (e.g. lorazepam) instead, lowest single dose, reviewed after each dose — benzodiazepines can themselves deepen delirium, so they are a last resort here too. If an antipsychotic is genuinely unavoidable in Parkinson's disease, quetiapine is the one used, on specialist advice.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: What is first-line for delirium due to alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back: Benzodiazepines, not antipsychotics. For established delirium tremens: oral lorazepam first-line; parenteral lorazepam (or haloperidol) if symptoms persist or oral is declined (NICE). Chlordiazepoxide is the agent for uncomplicated alcohol withdrawal, not established DT. Give parenteral thiamine alongside, before any glucose, to prevent Wernicke's.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: Do antipsychotics treat or prevent delirium?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back: No — antipsychotics do not treat or prevent delirium; they only manage severe distress until the cause is corrected. Avoid physical restraint and, where possible, sedation — they worsen delirium and cause harm.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: How is delirium prevented in at-risk inpatients?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back:
Multicomponent prevention:
  • orientation
  • early mobilisation
  • hydration/nutrition
  • sleep hygiene
  • sensory aids
  • pain control
  • avoiding constipation
  • and medication review to avoid deliriogenic drugs.
Also keep the person with a team familiar to them and avoid moving them between wards or rooms unless absolutely necessary (NICE). Prevention is more effective than treatment.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.front: What is the prognosis after an episode of delirium?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium.back: It often resolves as the cause is treated but can take weeks (and sometimes doesn't fully resolve). An episode is associated with increased mortality, longer admission, functional decline, and later dementia — so follow up and assess cognition after recovery.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.front: What are the Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards (DoLS)?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.back: The legal framework under the Mental Capacity Act 2005 for lawfully authorising the deprivation of liberty of a person who lacks capacity to consent to their care arrangements, in a hospital or care home, where those arrangements are in their best interests.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.front: Why does DoLS exist / which right does it protect?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.back: People with dementia, delirium, severe learning disability or brain injury may need to be kept somewhere and stopped from leaving for their own safety. Doing this without legal authorisation breaches their Article 5 (right to liberty). DoLS makes protective confinement lawful and scrutinised rather than arbitrary.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.front: To whom and in which settings does DoLS apply?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.back: Adults ≥18 who lack capacity to consent to their care/treatment arrangements, in a hospital or care home.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.front: What was the 'acid test' for a deprivation of liberty before June 2026?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.back:
A person WAS deprived of liberty if all three applied, the last two together forming the two-limb acid test:
  • (1) they lacked capacity to consent to the arrangements
  • (2) they were under continuous supervision and control
  • and (3) they were not free to leave.
This test was overruled by the Supreme Court in June 2026 and replaced by a multifactorial assessment — know it as history and as ward language, not as the current rule.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.front: Under the acid test, did it matter whether the person was content or the arrangements benevolent?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.back: No. Under the acid test it did not matter whether the person was content, whether the arrangements were benevolent/in their best interests, or the purpose — if the acid test was met and the person could not validly consent, authorisation was needed.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.front: What did the June 2026 Supreme Court ruling on deprivation of liberty decide?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.back: It overruled Cheshire West and removed the bright-line acid test as the sole determinant, with immediate, UK-wide effect and no transition period. In its place is a multifactorial assessment, and it revived that a person lacking Mental Capacity Act capacity may still give valid consent to their arrangements. Existing DoLS authorisations should be reviewed as soon as practicable, but leaving one in place pending review is not itself unlawful.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.front: What factors are weighed in the multifactorial test of a deprivation of liberty?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.back:
The acid-test factors remain relevant but are no longer sufficient; you weigh:
  • the type, duration, effects and manner of the restrictions
  • the normality of the setting (a near-normal home/family environment weighs against a deprivation)
  • the purpose of the measures
  • and whether the person objects or is content.
No single factor is determinative.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.front: Can a person who lacks Mental Capacity Act capacity ever avoid being deprived of liberty by consenting?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.back: Yes — a person lacking MCA capacity who can express genuine acceptance may be giving valid consent, meaning there is no deprivation of liberty. But this requires a basic awareness of their living arrangements sufficient to know and communicate whether they are happy with them. Passive compliance is not consent, and where there is serious doubt, valid consent must NOT be inferred — use DoLS or a court application.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.front: What is the difference between a restriction and a deprivation of liberty?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.back: A difference of degree and intensity, not kind. The more continuous, controlling and total the arrangements, the more likely they cross into a deprivation requiring authorisation.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.front: What are the Liberty Protection Safeguards (LPS), and what is their status?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.back: A scheme legislated in the Mental Capacity (Amendment) Act 2019 to replace DoLS with a streamlined, all-settings, age-16+ system. It has been repeatedly delayed and is still not implemented — a consultation on implementing it alongside an updated Code of Practice is being run, and it is not yet certain the scheme will proceed unchanged after the 2026 ruling. DoLS remains operational.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.front: What is the current operational position for authorising a deprivation of liberty (2026)?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.back: DoLS remains the operational process for hospitals and care homes (Court of Protection for other settings); it has not been abolished, and LPS is not yet implemented. When in doubt, continue using DoLS/Court of Protection processes.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.front: Who applies for a DoLS authorisation, and to whom?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.back: The Managing Authority (the hospital or care home) applies to the Supervisory Body (the local authority).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.front: What is an urgent DoLS authorisation?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.back: The managing authority can self-grant an urgent authorisation for up to 7 days while a standard authorisation is sought. The supervisory body can extend it by up to a further 7 days, so a maximum of 14.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.front: What is a standard DoLS authorisation and how long can it last?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.back: The supervisory body commissions the assessments and, if met, grants a standard authorisation that is time-limited (up to 12 months) and must be reviewed.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.front: Name the six assessments for a standard DoLS authorisation.
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.back:
• Age
  • mental capacity
  • mental health
  • best interests
  • eligibility (Mental Health Act interface)
  • and no-refusals (checking no valid ADRT/LPA/deputy decision conflicts).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.front: What safeguards and challenge rights does a person under DoLS have?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.back: They must have a Relevant Person's Representative and access to an Independent Mental Capacity Advocate (IMCA), and a right to challenge the authorisation in the Court of Protection under section 21A.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.front: How must any deprivation of liberty relate to the person's interests and freedom?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.back: It must always be the least restrictive option and in the person's best interests.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.front: How is a deprivation of liberty authorised in settings other than a hospital or care home (e.g. own home, supported living)?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.back: By the Court of Protection, not DoLS. Note that a DoLS authorisation makes the deprivation of liberty lawful — it does not authorise any specific treatment; treatment decisions still rest on capacity and best interests under the wider Mental Capacity Act.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.front: How is a deprivation of liberty handled for people under 18?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.back:
• 16-17-year-olds → the Court of Protection (the Mental Capacity Act applies from 16, but DoLS does not, as DoLS applies only to adults 18 and over).
  • Under 16 → the High Court's inherent jurisdiction.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.front: When might the Mental Health Act be the correct route instead of DoLS?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.back: If the person is detainable under the Mental Health Act for treatment of a mental disorder and objects, the MHA may be the correct route — the MHA/MCA interface is a recognised complexity.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.front: How does DoLS fit within the wider Mental Capacity Act framework?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivat.back: DoLS/LPS sit within the MCA — all five principles apply (presume capacity, support decision-making, unwise decisions aren't incapacity, best interests, least restrictive). It presupposes a 2-stage capacity assessment and a best-interests determination.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Elder Ab.front: What is adult safeguarding?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Elder Ab.back: The framework for protecting adults with care and support needs from abuse and neglect — statutorily defined as 'protecting an adult's right to live in safety, free from abuse and neglect'. Elder abuse is the commonest context, but it covers any adult made vulnerable by their care needs.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Elder Ab.front: Why does adult safeguarding matter?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Elder Ab.back:
• These adults are often dependent, isolated, and unable to protect themselves
  • the abuse is frequently hidden and by someone trusted (family carer, partner, paid staff)
  • and every clinician has a duty to recognise concerns and refer, even without proof.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Elder Ab.front: What is the pivotal difference between adult safeguarding and child protection?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Elder Ab.back: Capacity and autonomy. A child protection concern triggers protective action regardless of the child's wishes; an adult with capacity has the right to make unwise decisions, including declining help. Adult safeguarding is protection with the person, not to them.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Elder Ab.front: What is 'Making Safeguarding Personal'?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Elder Ab.back: The overarching, outcomes-focused, person-centred approach: work with the adult, respect their wishes and consent, and ask what they want to happen rather than impose a process — only overriding them where they lack capacity or others are at risk.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Elder Ab.front: What is the Section 42 (Care Act 2014) safeguarding duty?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Elder Ab.back:
The local authority must make a safeguarding enquiry where an adult (ALL THREE):
  • (1) has needs for care and support (whether or not the LA is meeting them)
  • (2) is experiencing, or at risk of, abuse or neglect
  • AND (3) as a result of those needs is unable to protect themselves against the abuse/neglect or the risk of it.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Elder Ab.front: Name the six principles of adult safeguarding (Care Act statutory guidance).
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Elder Ab.back:
• Empowerment (person-led, informed consent)
  • Prevention (act before harm)
  • Proportionality (least intrusive response)
  • Protection (support for those in greatest need)
  • Partnership (multi-agency working)
  • and Accountability (transparency).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Elder Ab.front: List the 10 categories of abuse in the Care Act guidance.
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Elder Ab.back:
• Physical
  • neglect/acts of omission
  • psychological/emotional
  • financial/material
  • sexual
  • discriminatory
  • organisational/institutional
  • domestic abuse
  • modern slavery
  • and self-neglect.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Elder Ab.front: Which is the commonest form of abuse, and which is especially common in elder abuse?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Elder Ab.back: Neglect / acts of omission (failure to provide care, food, heating, medication) is the commonest form. Financial/material abuse (theft, fraud, pressure over wills/benefits) is especially common in elder abuse.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Elder Ab.front: Which abuse category was newly included by the Care Act, and why is it notable?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Elder Ab.back: Self-neglect (neglecting personal hygiene, health, or surroundings) — a key change; it interacts with capacity and hoarding.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Elder Ab.front: What is organisational / institutional abuse?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Elder Ab.back: Poor care within a service or care home — neglectful routines, lack of dignity, and institutionalised poor practice.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Elder Ab.front: List the risk factors for elder abuse.
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Elder Ab.back:
• Cognitive impairment/dementia
  • physical dependence
  • social isolation
  • communication difficulties
  • a stressed or dependent carer
  • shared living with the abuser
  • and carer substance misuse/mental illness.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Elder Ab.front: What are the clinical red flags for elder abuse?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Elder Ab.back:
• Injury inconsistent with the explanation or with an unusual pattern
  • delayed presentation or injuries of different ages
  • unexplained financial changes (new 'friends', missing money, sudden will changes)
  • poor hygiene, malnutrition, dehydration, pressure sores (neglect)
  • fearfulness/withdrawal or a controlling carer who answers for the patient / won't leave the room
  • and frequent attendances, missed appointments, or behavioural change.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Elder Ab.front: Why is mental capacity described as 'the hinge' of adult safeguarding?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Elder Ab.back: You must assess capacity (MCA 2-stage test) for the specific decision (e.g. to accept help, to remain in a situation). Whether the adult has or lacks capacity determines whether their consent is needed to act — it is the pivotal step.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Elder Ab.front: If an adult being abused HAS capacity, how should you act?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Elder Ab.back:
Their consent is generally needed to act, and they may decline intervention (right to make unwise decisions). Continue to offer support. Exceptions (act without consent):
  • risk to others
  • a serious crime
  • undue coercion/duress (so consent isn't truly free)
  • or a public-interest justification.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Elder Ab.front: If an adult being abused LACKS capacity, how should you act?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Elder Ab.back: Act in their best interests, involving family/an Independent Mental Capacity Advocate; a safeguarding referral can be made without their consent.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Elder Ab.front: At what threshold should a clinician raise a safeguarding concern, and to whom?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Elder Ab.back: On reasonable suspicion, not proof — raise it with the local authority adult safeguarding team (discuss with your safeguarding lead if unsure).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Elder Ab.front: Outline what a clinician actually does when abuse is suspected.
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Elder Ab.back:
• (1) Ensure immediate safety (treat injuries, admit, call police if a crime/emergency).
  • (2) Raise a safeguarding concern (threshold = reasonable suspicion).
  • (3) Respect the adult's wishes/consent where they have capacity — but escalate regardless if others are at risk or a serious crime is involved.
  • (4) Document contemporaneously and factually; consider others at risk.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Elder Ab.front: How should suspected abuse be documented?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Elder Ab.back:
Carefully and factually:
  • history (verbatim where possible)
  • examination/body map
  • the capacity assessment
  • and the adult's expressed wishes.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Elder Ab.front: What are the rules on information sharing in safeguarding?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Elder Ab.back: Seek consent to share, but share without consent where the adult lacks capacity, others are at risk, or it is in the public interest — proportionate and Data Protection Act 2018/GDPR-compliant.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Elder Ab.front: What is a Safeguarding Adults Board (SAB)?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Elder Ab.back: A statutory multi-agency board (local authority, NHS, police) that coordinates and oversees local safeguarding.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Elder Ab.front: What is a Safeguarding Adults Review (SAR), and when is it commissioned?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Elder Ab.back: A review commissioned by the Safeguarding Adults Board when an adult with care/support needs dies or is seriously harmed and abuse/neglect is known or suspected, to learn lessons (not to allocate blame) — the adult equivalent of a child safeguarding practice review.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Elder Ab.front: Which other legal frameworks link to adult safeguarding?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Elder Ab.back:
• The Mental Capacity Act / DoLS
  • the Mental Health Act
  • the Domestic Abuse Act 2021
  • and Deprivation of Liberty processes
plus the Independent Mental Capacity Advocate for those lacking capacity with no one to represent them.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Falls As.front: Define a fall.
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Falls As.back: An event where a person unintentionally comes to rest on the ground or a lower level.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Falls As.front: Why do falls matter in older people?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Falls As.back:
Falls are a defining 'geriatric giant' — around a third of over-65s fall each year — and cause
  • fractures (especially hip)
  • head injury
  • 'long lie' complications
  • loss of confidence
  • functional decline
  • and loss of independence.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Falls As.front: What are the two aims when an older person falls?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Falls As.back:
• (1) Work out WHY this person fell (almost never one thing)
  • and (2) reduce the risk of the next fall.
A fall is both an injury to treat and a red flag for underlying illness.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Falls As.front: Why is a fall in an older person described as multifactorial?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Falls As.back: It is a syndrome, not a diagnosis — you don't look for THE cause; you find all the contributing factors and modify as many as you can. A fall is frequently the presenting sign of acute illness (sepsis, MI, stroke, delirium) — 'off legs' can be how pneumonia or a UTI shows up.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Falls As.front: What are the two headline changes in the current falls guidance (NICE)?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Falls As.back:
Two headline changes:
  • it now covers people aged 50–64 at higher risk (not just ≥65)
  • and it advises AGAINST using falls-risk-prediction tools (they lack sensitivity/specificity) — instead identify and act on individual risk factors.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Falls As.front: What is the first fork when assessing a 'fall' — and the key question to ask?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Falls As.back: Distinguish a mechanical/multifactorial fall from syncope (transient loss of consciousness). Always ask about loss of consciousness — an unwitnessed 'fall' may be a syncopal blackout.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Falls As.front: Which features suggest syncope rather than a mechanical fall, and what pathway do they trigger?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Falls As.back: Loss of consciousness, palpitations, exertional/chest symptoms, or no memory of the fall → the transient-loss-of-consciousness / cardiac pathway (ECG, lying/standing BP, cardiac workup) rather than only a falls assessment.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Falls As.front: What is the single best predictor of future falls?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Falls As.back: Previous falls. (Lower-limb muscle weakness is one of the strongest predictors too.) Ask every older patient: 'have you fallen in the past year?'

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Falls As.front: List the main intrinsic (patient) risk factors for falls.
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Falls As.back:
• Gait/balance/mobility problems and muscle weakness
  • previous falls and fear of falling
  • postural (orthostatic) hypotension
  • vision impairment
  • cognitive impairment/delirium
  • neurological (stroke, Parkinson's, neuropathy)
  • cardiovascular (arrhythmia, aortic stenosis, carotid sinus hypersensitivity)
  • foot problems/footwear
  • continence (nocturia, rushing to the toilet)
  • frailty/sarcopenia
  • acute illness
  • and alcohol.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Falls As.front: What are 'falls-risk-increasing drugs' (FRIDs)?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Falls As.back:
A core modifiable factor:
  • psychotropics (sedatives/hypnotics, benzodiazepines, antipsychotics, antidepressants — the big culprits)
  • antihypertensives, diuretics, nitrates (postural drop)
  • opioids, anticholinergics, antiepileptics
  • and polypharmacy itself (conventionally five or more regular medicines; four or more falls-risk-increasing drugs commonly triggers review).
Note the trap: falls risk alone is not a reason to stop anticoagulation in AF.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Falls As.front: List the extrinsic (environmental) risk factors for falls.
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Falls As.back:
Home hazards —
  • loose rugs
  • poor lighting
  • trailing cables
  • clutter
  • no grab rails
  • stairs
  • slippery floors
  • wet bathrooms.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Falls As.front: Who should receive a multifactorial falls assessment?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Falls As.back:
Anyone aged 65 or over — and anyone aged 50–64 with a condition that raises their risk (dementia, Parkinson's, stroke, arthritis, diabetes, learning disability) — who
  • presents after a fall
  • reports a fall in the past year
  • or has gait/balance problems.
Ask all older patients routinely: 'have you fallen in the past year?'

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Falls As.front: What are the components of a multifactorial falls assessment (NICE)?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Falls As.back:
• History of the fall(s) (context, frequency, LOC, prodrome, injuries, 'long lie')
  • gait and balance (observe walking; Timed Up-and-Go)
  • muscle strength/function
  • lying and standing BP
  • cardiovascular exam + ECG
  • vision
  • hearing
  • cognition and a delirium assessment
  • mood
  • dizziness (Dix-Hallpike if positional vertigo is suspected)
  • medication review (FRIDs, STOPP/START)
  • feet and footwear
  • continence
  • diet, fluids and weight loss
  • bone health/fracture risk (QFracture or FRAX)
  • review of long-term conditions
  • and home hazard assessment (OT).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Falls As.front: How is postural (orthostatic) hypotension defined?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Falls As.back: A fall of ≥20 mmHg systolic and/or ≥10 mmHg diastolic within 3 minutes of standing — or a systolic fall to below 90 mmHg, or reproduction of the patient's symptoms. Measure after ≥5 minutes lying, then at 1 and 3 minutes standing.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Falls As.front: How should gait/balance tools (e.g. Timed Up-and-Go) be used per NICE?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Falls As.back: They are useful for observing gait and balance deficits, but NOT as risk-prediction scores (NICE advises against falls-risk-prediction tools).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Falls As.front: Which investigations may be done to find reversible contributors and injuries after a fall?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Falls As.back: FBC, U&E, calcium, glucose, TFTs, vitamin D, B12 (reversible contributors), ECG, and imaging for injury (X-ray; CT head). On an anticoagulant, or an antiplatelet other than aspirin monotherapy, a head injury warrants a CT head within 8 hours even with no other indication — within 1 hour if presenting more than 8 hours after the injury (NICE).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Falls As.front: Which falls-prevention intervention has the strongest evidence?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Falls As.back: Strength and balance training — individually prescribed muscle-strengthening + balance programmes (Otago Exercise Programme, Tai Chi) — the single most effective measure.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Falls As.front: Besides exercise, what are the key elements of multifactorial falls management?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Falls As.back:
• Medication review (stop/reduce FRIDs — but do not stop anticoagulation in AF just because of falls risk)
  • treat postural hypotension (review drugs, hydration, slow position changes, compression, rarely fludrocortisone/midodrine)
  • vision (cataract surgery, refraction; caution with bifocals on stairs)
  • home hazard assessment/modification (OT)
  • cardiac treatment (arrhythmia; pacing for carotid sinus hypersensitivity)
  • bone protection
  • continence
  • addressing fear of falling
  • walking aids fitted by physio
  • telecare.
Keep people active — do not restrict activity or use restraint to prevent falls.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Falls As.front: What bone-protection measures reduce fracture risk in fallers?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Falls As.back: Assess fracture risk (QFracture or FRAX, ± DEXA) and offer a bisphosphonate where indicated; refer to the fracture liaison service after any fragility fracture. Add calcium and vitamin D only if dietary calcium is inadequate or the person is at risk of deficiency — vitamin D supplements are not given to prevent falls themselves (NICE).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Falls As.front: Outline the acute assessment immediately after a fall.
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Falls As.back:
A-E, treat injuries; look for
  • fracture (especially neck of femur — shortened, externally rotated leg)
  • head injury (a CT head within 8 hours if anticoagulated, even with no other indication)
  • and 'long lie' complications — check CK, U&E and urine for myoglobinuria and give IV fluids early.
Remember silver trauma: a low-energy fall can still cause major injury. Then find the trigger (obs + sepsis screen, ECG, lying/standing BP, glucose, bloods, medication review, neuro exam).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Falls As.front: What are the complications of a 'long lie' after a fall?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Falls As.back:
• Rhabdomyolysis
  • acute kidney injury
  • pressure sores
  • hypothermia
  • hypostatic pneumonia
  • and dehydration.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Falls As.front: What is the classic clinical sign of a neck-of-femur fracture after a fall?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Falls As.back: A shortened, externally rotated leg.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Frailty.front: What is frailty?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Frailty.back: A distinct health state of reduced physiological reserve across multiple body systems, leaving a person disproportionately vulnerable to decompensation after a minor stressor event.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Frailty.front: What is the 'stressor-decompensation' model of frailty?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Frailty.back: A minor event (a UTI, a new drug, a night in hospital) that a fit person shrugs off can, in a frail person, trigger a dramatic, disproportionate deterioration — a sudden fall in function that is slow (and sometimes incomplete) to recover.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Frailty.front: Why is frailty the unifying concept of geriatric medicine?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Frailty.back:
• It sits underneath falls, delirium, incontinence and the rationale for Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment
  • it predicts adverse outcomes better than age or any single diagnosis
  • and, crucially, it is not fixed — it can be identified, graded, and modified.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Frailty.front: Why do frail older people present with 'geriatric giants' rather than textbook illness?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Frailty.back:
Because reduced reserve means a stressor produces a non-specific decompensation rather than the classic features of the underlying illness (atypical presentation). The five frailty syndromes are
  • falls
  • immobility
  • delirium
  • incontinence
  • and susceptibility to medication side effects (e.g. confusion on codeine, hypotension on an antidepressant).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Frailty.front: What are the two models of frailty?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Frailty.back: The phenotype model (Fried) — frailty is a specific biological syndrome counted by 5 physical criteria — and the cumulative deficit model (Rockwood) — frailty is the accumulation of deficits, expressed as a Frailty Index.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Frailty.front: List the 5 criteria of the Fried frailty phenotype and the cut-offs.
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Frailty.back:
• (1) Unintentional weight loss (e.g. ≥4.5 kg/year)
  • (2) weakness (reduced grip strength)
  • (3) self-reported exhaustion
  • (4) slow walking speed
  • (5) low physical activity.
≥3 = frail; 1–2 = pre-frail; 0 = robust.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Frailty.front: What is the core biological feature underlying the Fried physical frailty phenotype?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Frailty.back: Sarcopenia — the age-related loss of muscle strength and mass — the biological engine of physical frailty. It is identified by low muscle strength (grip strength or chair-stand time) with confirmatory low muscle mass, which is why progressive resistance exercise plus adequate protein are central to management.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Frailty.front: How is the Rockwood cumulative deficit Frailty Index calculated?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Frailty.back: Frailty Index = (number of deficits present) / (number of deficits assessed), giving a score from 0 to 1 — the closer to 1.0, the frailer. Deficits include symptoms, signs, diseases, disabilities and psychosocial factors.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Frailty.front: What is the electronic Frailty Index (eFI)?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Frailty.back: An auto-calculated Frailty Index derived from 36 deficits coded in GP records, built into the main UK primary-care record systems and used to case-find frailty at population scale. Bands: ≤0.12 fit; >0.12–0.24 mild; >0.24–0.36 moderate; >0.36 severe — a flag prompts clinical confirmation, not an automatic label.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Frailty.front: What is the Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS)?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Frailty.back: Rockwood's practical bedside scale — a 9-point clinical-judgement scale, scored after a holistic assessment, that maps a person's baseline function onto a level of frailty. It is the workhorse in UK acute/emergency settings.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Frailty.front: What do Clinical Frailty Scale scores 1–3 represent?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Frailty.back:
• 1 = Very fit (robust, active, exercises regularly)
  • 2 = Fit/well (no active disease, less fit than 1)
  • 3 = Managing well (medical problems well controlled, not regularly active).
Anchor: 1–3 = fit.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Frailty.front: What does Clinical Frailty Scale score 4 represent?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Frailty.back: 4 = Vulnerable (very mild frailty) — not dependent, but symptoms limit activities; 'slowed up'. Anchor: 4 = vulnerable/pre-frail.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Frailty.front: What do Clinical Frailty Scale scores 5 and 6 represent?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Frailty.back:
• 5 = Mildly frail — needs help with IADLs (finances, transport, shopping, heavy housework).
  • 6 = Moderately frail — needs help with outside activities and some ADLs (bathing, dressing).
Anchor: 5–6 = mild-moderate frailty.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Frailty.front: What do Clinical Frailty Scale scores 7–9 represent?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Frailty.back:
• 7 = Severely frail (completely dependent for personal care; stable)
  • 8 = Very severely frail (completely dependent, approaching end of life, wouldn't recover from minor illness)
  • 9 = Terminally ill (life expectancy <6 months, not otherwise evidently frail).
Anchor: 7–9 = severe.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Frailty.front: What is the key caveat when scoring the Clinical Frailty Scale?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Frailty.back: Score the BASELINE function (usually ~2 weeks before the current acute illness), NOT the acute state. It is validated in adults ≥65 — do not use it in younger adults, or in people with stable long-standing disability (e.g. cerebral palsy), learning disability or autism; assess those patients individually. CFS ≥5 is the usual threshold to trigger a frailty pathway and CGA.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Frailty.front: Why does the Clinical Frailty Scale matter, and how should it be used in decisions?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Frailty.back: It predicts mortality, length of stay and outcomes and guides escalation/ceiling-of-treatment, resuscitation and shared decisions about major interventions (surgery, critical care, TAVI) — always alongside clinical judgement and the patient's wishes, never as a sole determinant. It is not an eligibility criterion for stroke thrombolysis or thrombectomy, where pre-stroke function is graded with the modified Rankin Scale.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Frailty.front: Name other frailty identification tools besides the CFS.
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Frailty.back: Gait speed (>5 s to walk 4 m suggests frailty) and the timed up-and-go — but do not use a physical performance tool in someone who is acutely unwell (NICE); use a history-based tool such as the CFS instead. Also the PRISMA-7 questionnaire (≥3 suggests frailty); the FRAIL scale, Edmonton Frail Scale, and Hospital Frailty Risk Score (from admin data).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Frailty.front: What are the consequences of frailty?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Frailty.back: Increased risk of falls, delirium, immobility, incontinence (geriatric giants), fluctuating disability, iatrogenic harm/polypharmacy sensitivity, hospital admission, longer stays, institutionalisation, and death — and atypical presentations of illness.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Frailty.front: What is the cornerstone of frailty management?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Frailty.back: Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment — the multidimensional, MDT process that turns a frailty label into a coordinated plan.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Frailty.front: Which intervention has the strongest evidence in frailty?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Frailty.back: Exercise — progressive resistance (strength) + balance training — which improves muscle mass and function and reduces falls.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Frailty.front: What are the key non-exercise elements of frailty management?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Frailty.back:
• Nutrition (adequate protein/calories, treat malnutrition, correct vitamin D, address sarcopenia)
  • medication review to rationalise polypharmacy and stop falls-risk-increasing/anticholinergic drugs (STOPP/START)
  • optimise chronic disease and reversible contributors (anaemia, thyroid, depression, sensory impairment)
  • and advance care planning (ceilings of care, ReSPECT) plus social/community support.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Frailty.front: Is frailty a fixed, irreversible decline?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Frailty.back: No — frailty is dynamic: it can be stabilised or improved. The goal is maintaining/restoring function and independence, not just managing decline.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.front: What is hyperthermia, and how does it differ from fever?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.back: Hyperthermia is a raised core temperature from a failure of thermoregulation — heat load exceeds heat dissipation, with a normal hypothalamic set-point. In fever the set-point is deliberately raised by pyrogens. Consequently antipyretics do NOT work in hyperthermia — the treatment is physical cooling.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.front: Why are antipyretics (paracetamol/NSAIDs) ineffective in hyperthermia?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.back: Because the hypothalamic set-point is normal (the problem is failed heat loss, not a pyrogen-raised set-point). Antipyretics only lower a raised set-point, so they don't help — and may be harmful (hepatic/renal). Physical cooling is the treatment.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.front: What are the two big branches of hyperthermia?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.back:
• Environmental heat illness (heat exhaustion → heat stroke)
  • and drug-induced/metabolic hyperthermia (neuroleptic malignant syndrome, serotonin syndrome, malignant hyperthermia, anticholinergic/sympathomimetic toxicity, thyroid storm).
The unifying emergency principle is rapid cooling + supportive care + treat the cause.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.front: What single feature distinguishes heat stroke from heat exhaustion?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.back:
Central nervous system dysfunction (altered mental state).
  • Heat exhaustion: core temp usually <40degC, CNS intact.
  • Heat stroke: >40degC + altered consciousness (confusion, seizures, coma) — a life-threatening emergency.
Hyperthermia + confusion = heat stroke until proven otherwise.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.front: Contrast classic (non-exertional) and exertional heat stroke.
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.back:
• Classic: elderly/chronically ill/very young, triggered by a heatwave, often dry hot skin (sweating absent), associated with isolation/immobility, higher mortality.
  • Exertional: young/fit (athletes, soldiers), strenuous exertion in heat, often still sweating (a trap), commonly complicated by rhabdomyolysis/AKI.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.front: List the risk factors for heat stroke.
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.back:
• Extremes of age
  • drugs — anticholinergics, antipsychotics, antihistamines, diuretics, beta-blockers, stimulants/sympathomimetics
  • alcohol
  • dehydration
  • obesity
  • cardiovascular disease
  • immobility/social isolation
  • and housing that overheats — top-floor or south-facing flats, poor ventilation, an inability to open windows safely.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.front: What are the clinical features and complications of heat stroke?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.back:
• Core temp >40degC + CNS dysfunction (confusion → seizures → coma)
  • tachycardia
  • hypotension (may mimic septic shock)
  • tachypnoea.
Complications:
  • rhabdomyolysis → AKI
  • DIC
  • hepatic failure
  • ARDS
  • electrolyte derangement
  • multi-organ failure.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.front: What is the classic clinical clue to rhabdomyolysis after exertion in heat?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.back: Dark urine (myoglobinuria) after exertion in heat — check creatine kinase and watch for acute kidney injury.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.front: Which investigations are important in suspected heat stroke?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.back:
• Core (rectal) temperature — essential and continuous
  • bloods: U&E, creatine kinase, LFTs, coagulation/DIC screen, FBC, glucose, ABG, lactate
  • urinalysis (myoglobinuria)
  • ECG.
Rule out mimics — sepsis (cultures) and the drug-induced syndromes.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.front: What is the single most important, life-saving intervention in heat stroke?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.back: Rapid cooling — begin immediately, don't wait for tests. Goal: bring the core temperature below about 39degC within the first 30 minutes, then stop active cooling at around 38.5degC to avoid overshoot.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.front: Which cooling method is most effective for EXERTIONAL heat stroke (young patient)?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.back: Cold/ice-water immersion — the most effective method (near-zero fatality if done fast).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.front: Which cooling method is preferred for CLASSIC heat stroke (frail elderly)?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.back: Evaporative cooling (spray tepid water + fans) +/- ice packs to groin/axillae/neck — better tolerated in frail patients. Aim to get the core below about 39degC within 30 minutes, then stop active cooling at around 38.5degC to avoid overshoot.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.front: Besides cooling, what supportive management does heat stroke require?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.back:
• A-E resuscitation: oxygen, cool IV crystalloid for hypotension and rhabdomyolysis (which also contributes to cooling), airway protection if reduced consciousness
  • treat complications — early generous fluids are the mainstay for rhabdomyolysis and its AKI (urinary alkalinisation is not routine and is a specialist decision), manage DIC, benzodiazepines for seizures
  • manage shivering and agitation with benzodiazepines (shivering generates heat)
  • avoid physical restraints
  • ICU for multi-organ failure.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.front: How is heat exhaustion managed?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.back: Move to a cool place, rest, oral/IV rehydration, remove excess clothing, and cool — recognise and treat it before it progresses to heat stroke.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.front: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome — trigger, onset, features and treatment?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.back:
• Trigger: antipsychotics (or dopamine withdrawal)
  • Onset: slow (days)
  • Features: 'lead-pipe' rigidity, bradyreflexia, markedly raised creatine kinase, autonomic instability
  • Treatment: stop the causative drug, supportive care with IV fluids and active cooling, +/- dantrolene or bromocriptine in severe cases.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.front: Serotonin syndrome — trigger, onset, features and treatment?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.back:
• Trigger: serotonergic drugs (SSRIs, MAOIs, tramadol, linezolid)
  • Onset: fast (hours)
  • Features: clonus, hyperreflexia (especially lower limbs), agitation, dilated pupils, diarrhoea
  • Treatment: stop the drug; benzodiazepines; cyproheptadine.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.front: Malignant hyperthermia — trigger, features and treatment?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.back:
• Trigger: volatile anaesthetics + suxamethonium (RYR1 mutation), within minutes-hours of anaesthesia
  • Features: masseter/generalised rigidity, rising CO₂, markedly raised creatine kinase, hyperkalaemia
  • Treatment: dantrolene (+ stop the agent).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.front: Anticholinergic toxicity — features and how it differs from the rigidity syndromes?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.back: 'Hot as a hare, dry as a bone, red as a beet, mad as a hatter, blind as a bat' — dry skin, dilated pupils, urinary retention, and NO rigidity. Treatment is supportive + cooling (physostigmine in selected cases).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.front: Give the quick discriminators for the hyperthermia syndromes.
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.back:
• Rigidity + antipsychotic + slow onset = neuroleptic malignant syndrome
  • clonus/hyperreflexia + serotonergic drug + fast onset = serotonin syndrome
