  • anaesthetic + rigidity + rising CO₂ = malignant hyperthermia (→ dantrolene)
  • dry, flushed, dilated pupils, no rigidity = anticholinergic.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.front: What public-health/geriatric measures prevent heat illness during heatwaves?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.back:
• Hydration
  • cool environment/shade
  • avoid peak heat
  • light clothing
  • check on isolated elderly and those on culprit drugs
  • review diuretics/anticholinergics
  • and heed the Heat-Health Alerts (UKHSA).
In winter the same applies in reverse — Cold-Health Alerts are the trigger to check on isolated older people, and hypothermia is as much a social diagnosis (cold housing, fuel poverty, self-neglect) as a medical one.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.front: Define hypothermia.
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.back: A core body temperature below 35degC, from heat loss exceeding heat production. The frail, isolated, immobile elderly are hit hardest (often indoors in winter, after a fall and 'long lie').

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.front: What are the two counterintuitive, high-yield rules of hypothermia?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.back:
• (1) 'No one is dead until they're warm and dead' — continue resuscitation through rewarming, as the cold heart may be viable.
  • (2) Handle gently and rewarm the core first — rough handling or peripheral rewarming can precipitate a fatal arrhythmia or 'afterdrop'.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.front: How is hypothermia staged by core temperature, and what is the clinical picture of each?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.back:
• Mild (32–35degC): shivering present, tachycardia, tachypnoea, confusion, ataxia, cold diuresis.
  • Moderate (28–32degC): shivering STOPS, bradycardia, reduced consciousness, dilated pupils, Osborn (J) waves, AF.
  • Severe (<28degC): coma, areflexia, fixed dilated pupils, hypotension, VF/asystole risk — may appear dead.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.front: Why is shivering a favourable sign in hypothermia?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.back: Shivering means the patient is still mild (>~32degC) and generating heat. When shivering stops, they have dropped into the dangerous moderate/severe range.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.front: Why is a core temperature below 30degC particularly dangerous?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.back: The myocardium becomes electrically unstable and prone to ventricular fibrillation, so everything below that point is about minimal handling and careful, staged rewarming.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.front: List the causes/risk factors for hypothermia.
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.back:
• Environmental exposure (cold, immersion, inadequate clothing/heating)
  • elderly (impaired thermoregulation, immobility, isolation, cold housing, fall + long lie)
  • reduced heat production (hypothyroidism, hypopituitarism, hypoglycaemia, malnutrition, sepsis)
  • impaired awareness (alcohol, sedatives, dementia)
  • extensive burns/erythroderma, spinal injury
  • and neonates (high surface-area-to-volume ratio).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.front: What is 'paradoxical undressing'?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.back: Removing clothes due to a confused sensation of warmth — a recognised feature of severe hypothermia.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.front: Why does hypothermia cause hypovolaemia?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.back: Cold diuresis — cold-induced diuresis depletes intravascular volume, so warmed IV fluids are needed.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.front: What kind of thermometer is needed to diagnose hypothermia?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.back: A low-reading rectal probe, or an oesophageal probe in the intubated patient (rectal readings lag behind the true core during rewarming) — a standard thermometer won't read low enough, and infrared tympanic and forehead thermometers are unreliable in a cold, vasoconstricted patient.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.front: What is the characteristic ECG finding in hypothermia?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.back: The Osborn (J) wave — a positive deflection at the J point (QRS-ST junction), whose size grows as the core temperature falls, usually visible below about 32degC but not present in every patient, so a normal J point does not exclude hypothermia. Don't mistake it for a STEMI.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.front: What ECG changes and arrhythmia sequence occur in hypothermia?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.back: Osborn (J) waves, bradycardia, prolonged PR/QRS/QT, and AF — with the classic sequence sinus bradycardia → AF → ventricular fibrillation → asystole.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.front: Which blood result predicts non-survival and guides stopping resuscitation in hypothermia?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.back: A markedly raised potassium (around 12 mmol/L or above) in hypothermic cardiac arrest carries a very poor outcome and is one factor a specialist team weighs when deciding about extracorporeal rewarming — never used on its own, and the decision to stop is a senior one. Also check glucose, U&E, TFTs and cortisol (myxoedema coma, adrenal insufficiency), FBC, coagulation, blood gas, creatine kinase, amylase, cultures and toxicology.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.front: What are the general management principles for hypothermia?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.back:
• A-E with minimal handling (rough movement can precipitate VF)
  • remove wet clothing, insulate, warm environment
  • warmed humidified oxygen and warmed IV fluids (for cold-diuresis hypovolaemia)
  • continuous cardiac monitoring
  • and treat the underlying cause.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.front: Why must you rewarm the core/trunk before the extremities?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.back: Peripheral rewarming causes 'afterdrop' — vasodilated cold limbs return cold, acidotic blood to the core, causing a further temperature drop and hypotension.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.front: What are the rewarming methods matched to severity?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.back:
• Mild - passive external (remove wet clothes, blankets, warm room; a slow gradual rise over hours is expected).
  • Moderate - active external (forced warm air, heating blankets, warm packs to the trunk not limbs — these can burn cold, insensate skin).
  • Severe - active internal/core (warmed humidified oxygen and warmed IV fluids on the ward; body-cavity lavage and extracorporeal rewarming/ECMO in specialist settings for arrested or refractory cases — the most effective).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.front: What are the key Advanced Life Support modifications for cardiac arrest in hypothermia?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.back:
'No one is dead until warm and dead' — continue CPR through rewarming. Check a central pulse and breathing for up to one minute before diagnosing arrest, since the cold patient's pulse is very hard to feel.
  • Below ~30degC: withhold arrest drugs and limit defibrillation to 3 shocks until the core rises above ~30degC.
  • 30–35degC: double the interval between drug doses.
Continue until the core is above 35degC or a senior decision is made; consider ECMO transfer. Hypothermia is one of the reversible 4 Hs.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.front: Why are fixed dilated pupils and rigidity unreliable in confirming death in hypothermia?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.back: In hypothermia fixed dilated pupils, apparent rigidity and cold stiffening are not reliable signs of death — the patient may recover with rewarming. Continue resuscitation until the core temperature is above 35degC, or a senior decision is made.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.front: What are the complications of hypothermia?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.back: Ventricular arrhythmias, aspiration pneumonia, rhabdomyolysis/acute kidney injury, pancreatitis, coagulopathy — cold impairs clotting enzymes and platelets, and because the lab warms the sample to 37degC the clotting screen can look falsely normal — afterdrop, hypotension during rewarming, and frostbite/cold injury to the extremities.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.front: What is meant by malnutrition in this context?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.back: Under-nutrition — a deficiency of energy, protein and micronutrients. It is common, under-recognised, and reversible, and is hugely prevalent in the frail and hospitalised elderly.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.front: Why does malnutrition matter in older people?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.back: It drives sarcopenia → frailty → falls, impairs wound healing and immune function, and worsens recovery. It is easy to screen for (MUST) and often treatable ('food first'), yet routinely missed — and correcting it too fast causes refeeding syndrome. Distinguish simple undernutrition, which intake corrects, from disease-related cachexia, which feeding alone does not reverse.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.front: Why is malnutrition described as a 'marker' rather than an isolated problem?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.back: It is a downstream marker of an underlying cause — poor dentition, dysphagia, depression, dementia, social isolation, poverty, chronic disease, or the anorexia of ageing. The task is: screen → identify the cause → support intake → escalate → do it safely.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.front: List the causes of reduced intake contributing to malnutrition.
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.back:
• Poor appetite ('anorexia of ageing')
  • depression
  • dementia
  • poor dentition/ill-fitting dentures
  • dysphagia (stroke, Parkinson's)
  • altered taste/smell
  • and nausea.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.front: List the social and iatrogenic contributors to malnutrition.
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.back:
• Social: isolation, bereavement, immobility, poverty ('heat or eat'), inability to shop/cook, reliance on carers.
  • Iatrogenic: polypharmacy (nausea, dry mouth, anorexia), nil-by-mouth episodes, restrictive diets.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.front: Which conditions increase nutritional requirements or losses?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.back:
• Acute illness
  • cancer
  • chronic disease (COPD, heart failure, CKD)
  • infection
  • malabsorption (coeliac, IBD, pancreatic)
  • hyperthyroidism
  • and surgery/wounds.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.front: What is the MUST tool, and what three components does it score?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.back:
The Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool — the validated UK 5-step screen. It scores:
  • (1) BMI
  • (2) unplanned weight loss over 3–6 months
  • and (3) an acute disease effect.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.front: How is BMI scored in MUST?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.back:
• 0 = BMI >20
  • 1 = 18.5–20
  • 2 = <18.5.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.front: How is unplanned weight loss (3–6 months) scored in MUST?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.back:
• 0 = <5%
  • 1 = 5–10%
  • 2 = >10%.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.front: How is the acute disease effect scored in MUST?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.back: Add 2 if the patient is acutely ill and there has been (or is likely to be) no nutritional intake for >5 days.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.front: How is the total MUST score interpreted?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.back:
• 0 = low risk (routine rescreen)
  • 1 = medium risk (observe / food diary)
  • ≥2 = high risk (treat — dietitian, nutrition plan).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.front: When should nutritional screening with MUST be done?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.back:
Screen all adults
  • on hospital admission
  • on admission to a care home
  • at first outpatient appointment
  • on GP registration
  • and when clinically concerned.
Rescreen weekly in hospital inpatients and at least monthly in care homes. Malnourished = BMI <18.5, or >10% unintentional loss in 3–6 months, or BMI <20 with >5% loss (NICE).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.front: Is serum albumin a reliable marker of nutritional status?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.back: No — albumin reflects illness/inflammation, not nutrition, and is not a reliable nutritional marker.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.front: What clinical signs suggest malnutrition?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.back:
• Weight loss
  • loose clothing/dentures/rings
  • muscle wasting (temporal, thenar)
  • poor wound healing
  • fatigue
  • low mood
  • and recurrent infection.
Suspect sarcopenia — loss of muscle mass and strength — from weak grip, slow gait and difficulty rising from a chair; it needs resistance exercise as well as nutrition. Do not attribute unexplained weight loss to ageing: sweep for red flags and refer on a suspected-cancer pathway where indicated.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.front: What is the first-line ('Food First') approach to managing malnutrition?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.back:
• Food fortification (add cream, butter, cheese, milk powder, oils to normal food to boost energy/protein density)
  • small, frequent, energy-dense meals + nourishing snacks and drinks
  • and addressing barriers (dentures/dental care, texture-modified diet for dysphagia, feeding assistance, social mealtimes, treat depression, manage nausea, review culprit drugs).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.front: When are Oral Nutritional Supplements (ONS) used, and how?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.back: When food-first measures alone do not meet requirements — for people who are malnourished or at risk. In high-risk patients they are started alongside dietary fortification, not held back until food-first has failed. Prescribed against ACBS indications, with a goal, and reviewed and stopped as intake recovers.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.front: When is enteral tube feeding (NG/PEG) used?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.back: When the gut works but oral intake is unsafe or inadequate (e.g. stroke dysphagia) — NG tube short-term, PEG if long-term. NG safety: confirm position after placement and before every feed, flush or medicine — aspirate and check pH is 1–5.5; if above 5.5 or no aspirate, do not feed and get a chest X-ray reported. Never auscultate — feeding through a misplaced tube is a Never Event (NHS England).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.front: When is parenteral nutrition indicated?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.back: Only if the gastrointestinal tract is non-functional or inaccessible (obstruction, short bowel, ileus). It carries infection/line risks.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.front: What is the position on tube feeding in advanced dementia?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.back: Tube feeding does NOT improve outcomes in advanced dementia — it does not improve survival, prevent aspiration or heal pressure ulcers — and is generally not recommended. Clinically assisted nutrition and hydration is a medical treatment, so assess capacity, honour a valid advance decision, and otherwise decide in best interests with the MDT and those close to the patient. Food and drink offered by mouth is basic care and always continued — comfort/hand feeding is preferred.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.front: What is refeeding syndrome?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.back: In a chronically starved patient, reintroducing carbohydrate causes a surge of insulin → cells rapidly take up phosphate, potassium, magnesium and glucose (plus thiamine consumption) → dangerous falls in serum phosphate/potassium/magnesium and fluid shifts → arrhythmias, cardiac/respiratory failure, seizures, Wernicke's, death.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.front: What is the biochemical hallmark of refeeding syndrome?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.back: Hypophosphataemia (also falls in potassium and magnesium).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.front: What are the NICE high-risk criteria for refeeding syndrome?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.back:
ONE OR MORE of:
  • BMI <16
  • unintentional weight loss >15% in 3–6 months
  • little/no intake >10 days
  • low potassium/phosphate/magnesium before feeding.
OR TWO OR MORE of:
  • BMI <18.5
  • weight loss >10% in 3–6 months
  • little/no intake >5 days
  • history of alcohol misuse or certain drugs (insulin, chemo, antacids, diuretics).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.front: How is refeeding syndrome prevented/managed?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.back:
• Start feeding LOW and SLOW — max ~10 kcal/kg/day, building over ~4–7 days (5 kcal/kg/day if extreme, e.g. BMI <14)
  • give thiamine and vitamin B co strong before and during feeding (prevents Wernicke's)
  • and supplement potassium, phosphate and magnesium from the start of feeding, monitoring them daily and replacing as needed, with fluid balance and cardiac monitoring.
Do not delay feeding to pre-correct low levels.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.front: What is a neck of femur (hip) fracture, and why does it matter?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.back: The defining orthogeriatric emergency — a fragility fracture in a frail older person that is both an orthopaedic problem (fix the bone) and a whole-person medical crisis. It is common and lethal (roughly 1 in 15 to 1 in 10 die within 30 days, a quarter to a third within a year), and outcomes depend more on peri-operative medical care than on the operation itself.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.front: Why is a hip fracture called a 'sentinel event of frailty'?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.back:
The fracture will be fixed, but the patient often dies of the complications —
  • delirium
  • pneumonia
  • pressure sores
  • VTE
  • deconditioning.
Peri-operative care is about protecting the whole patient through surgery and launching rapid rehabilitation via a shared-care orthogeriatric team.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.front: What anatomical distinction determines the operation for a hip fracture, and why?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.back:
Intracapsular vs extracapsular (relative to the hip joint capsule).
  • Intracapsular fractures risk disrupting the retrograde blood supply to the femoral head → high avascular necrosis risk
  • extracapsular fractures leave the head's blood supply intact.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.front: How is an UNDISPLACED intracapsular hip fracture managed?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.back: Internal fixation (or hemiarthroplasty if the patient is unfit).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.front: How is a DISPLACED intracapsular hip fracture managed?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.back: Replace the joint — total hip replacement or hemiarthroplasty (because the disrupted retrograde blood supply makes avascular necrosis/non-union likely if fixed).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.front: When is total hip replacement favoured over hemiarthroplasty for a displaced intracapsular fracture?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.back:
• If the patient walked independently outdoors with no more than a stick
  • has no condition or comorbidity making the procedure unsuitable
  • and is expected to carry out activities of daily living independently beyond 2 years (NICE).
Cognitive impairment alone is not an automatic exclusion — it is weighed as one comorbidity among others.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.front: How is a stable inter-trochanteric (extracapsular) fracture managed?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.back: With a dynamic hip screw (DHS).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.front: How is a sub-trochanteric or reverse-oblique/transverse (extracapsular) fracture managed?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.back: With an intramedullary nail.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.front: What is the Garden classification?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.back: A classification of intracapsular fractures I-IV (I = incomplete → II = complete undisplaced → III = partially displaced → IV = fully displaced).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.front: What are the clinical and radiological signs of a hip fracture?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.back: Pain and a shortened + externally rotated leg; X-ray shows a disrupted Shenton's line. If X-ray is normal but occult fracture is suspected, use MRI (or CT).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.front: What immediate pre-operative care does a hip-fracture patient need on admission?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.back:
A-E, resuscitation, and treat what caused the fall (often a presentation of acute illness — sepsis, MI, arrhythmia, stroke, delirium).
  • Bloods, ECG, CXR, group & save, X-ray
  • IV fluids
  • treat anaemia
  • pressure area care from arrival
  • VTE assessment.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.front: What analgesia is recommended pre-operatively for a hip fracture?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.back:
Early, cognition-sparing analgesia:
  • regular paracetamol 6-hourly
  • adding an immediate-release opioid if that is not enough
  • and a fascia iliaca compartment block if paracetamol plus an opioid is still insufficient or to limit the opioid dose (nerve blocks reduce delirium, respiratory depression and constipation).
Do not use NSAIDs, and never use a block as a substitute for early surgery — surgery is the definitive analgesia.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.front: Within what timeframe should hip-fracture surgery be performed?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.back: On the day of, or the day after, admission — within ~36 hours, on a planned trauma list. This is the single most important peri-operative target; delay worsens mortality, delirium, and pressure sores.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.front: What are ACCEPTABLE (correctable) reasons to delay hip-fracture surgery?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.back:
• Severe anaemia
  • uncontrolled heart failure
  • significant electrolyte/coagulation abnormality
  • uncontrolled diabetes
  • or a chest infection needing treatment.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.front: What are NOT acceptable reasons to delay hip-fracture surgery?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.back:
• Minor or uncorrectable derangements
  • that it is simply 'out of hours'
  • waiting passively for anticoagulation to wear off — reverse warfarin actively with vitamin K and plan DOAC timing instead
  • and waiting for a routine pre-operative echocardiogram, which should only be requested if it will change management.
Do not use traction routinely in place of operating.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.front: What is the orthogeriatric shared-care model, and its benefits?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.back: The patient is admitted under a formal orthogeriatric/shared-care pathway with comprehensive geriatric assessment within 72 hours; the geriatrician and orthopaedic team jointly manage pre-op optimisation, comorbidity, post-op complications and rehab. It reduces mortality, length of stay, and complications.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.front: Is spinal or general anaesthesia superior for hip-fracture surgery?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.back: Either is acceptable — evidence shows no clear superiority of spinal over general for survival or recovery (correcting the common misconception that spinal is always better).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.front: What is the goal for weight-bearing and mobilisation after hip-fracture surgery?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.back: Operate to allow immediate full weight-bearing where the fixation permits, and mobilise the day after surgery (physiotherapy), then at least daily — central to preventing deconditioning, VTE, pneumonia and pressure sores.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.front: What does post-operative multidisciplinary rehabilitation involve?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.back: The Hip Fracture Programme — physiotherapy, occupational therapy, dietitian, nursing, orthogeriatrics — goal-oriented, aiming to return the patient to their pre-fracture residence and function.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.front: Which routine post-operative screening/care is needed after a hip fracture?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.back:
• Screen for delirium with the 4AT on admission and again after surgery and run the prevention bundle
  • continue VTE prophylaxis (low molecular weight heparin restarted 6–12 hours post-operatively and continued for a month)
  • screen nutrition (MUST)
  • and attend to continence, skin and pressure care (catheter avoidance) and bowel care
— with adequate analgesia to enable mobilisation.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.front: What secondary prevention must not be missed after a hip fracture?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.back:
• Bone health: the fracture IS the diagnosis of osteoporosis — start vitamin D (with calcium if dietary intake is inadequate) plus a bisphosphonate before discharge, without waiting for a DEXA scan.
  • Falls: a hip fracture is a fall until proven otherwise — do a multifactorial falls assessment.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.front: What surgical complications should be anticipated after a hip fracture?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.back:
• Avascular necrosis (intracapsular)
  • non-union
  • infection
  • dislocation/implant failure
  • and peri-prosthetic fracture.
(Medical complications include delirium, pneumonia, VTE, pressure ulcers, AKI, UTI, constipation and deconditioning.)

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.front: What is polypharmacy, and how is it commonly defined?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.back: The concurrent use of multiple medications — commonly defined as ≥5 regular medicines. It is a central problem of geriatric medicine as older, multimorbid patients accumulate drugs across decades and specialties.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.front: Why does polypharmacy matter?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.back:
Each additional drug raises the risk of
  • adverse drug reactions
  • interactions
  • falls
  • delirium
  • hospital admission
  • poor adherence
  • and prescribing cascades (where a drug's side-effect is treated with another drug).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.front: What is a prescribing cascade?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.back: When a drug's side-effect is misinterpreted as a new condition and treated with another drug (e.g. amlodipine causes ankle oedema → a diuretic is added), compounding polypharmacy.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.front: Distinguish appropriate from problematic polypharmacy.
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.back:
• Appropriate: multiple drugs, each with a valid, current indication and net benefit (continue + monitor).
  • Problematic (inappropriate): drugs that are unnecessary, harmful, duplicated, or whose harms outweigh benefits (structured review → deprescribe/adjust).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.front: Is polypharmacy inherently bad? What is the goal of review?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.back: No — a patient with several conditions may appropriately need several drugs. The problem is problematic polypharmacy. The goal is not to blindly cut pills but to optimise the regimen: stop what's harmful/pointless (STOPP) and start what's beneficial but missing (START). Deprescribing is an active, evidence-based intervention, not neglect.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.front: What does STOPP stand for and flag?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.back: Screening Tool of Older Persons' Prescriptions — it flags Potentially Inappropriate Medications (PIMs), i.e. drugs to consider stopping.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.front: What does START stand for and flag?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.back: Screening Tool to Alert to Right Treatment — it flags Potential Prescribing Omissions (PPOs), i.e. beneficial drugs that are missing and should be started.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.front: What is the key insight that STOPP/START captures?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.back: Inappropriate prescribing is bidirectional: under-prescribing (a missed statin post-MI, no bone protection after a fragility fracture, no anticoagulation in AF) is as much an error as over-prescribing.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.front: What is notable about STOPP/START version 3?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.back: It expanded to 190 criteria (from 114 in version 2), with dedicated sections for falls-risk drugs, opioids, and anticholinergics. Using STOPP/START reduces adverse drug reactions, inappropriate prescribing and medication costs.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.front: What pharmacokinetic changes make older people vulnerable to drugs?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.back: Reduced renal clearance → drug accumulation. Serum creatinine is misleading when muscle mass is low, and reported eGFR is normalised to body surface area, so in small frail patients it overstates true clearance — dose narrow-therapeutic-index and renally cleared drugs on creatinine clearance (Cockcroft-Gault) (BNF). Also altered hepatic metabolism, reduced albumin (more free drug), and altered body composition (increased fat → longer half-life of lipophilic drugs like benzodiazepines).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.front: What pharmacodynamic change and 'frailty multiplier' increase drug harm in older people?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.back: Increased sensitivity (e.g. to CNS depressants, anticholinergics, warfarin). The frailty multiplier: reduced reserve means small drug effects cause big clinical harm (a sedative trivial in a fit adult causes a fall/delirium in the frail).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.front: List the consequences of problematic polypharmacy.
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.back:
• Adverse drug reactions (a major cause of hospital admission in the elderly)
  • falls
  • delirium/confusion
  • acute kidney injury
  • GI bleeding
  • prescribing cascades
  • poor adherence
  • drug interactions
  • and increased mortality and cost.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.front: Give common STOPP examples (drugs to consider stopping).
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.back:
• Benzodiazepines/Z-drugs (falls/confusion) and long-term antipsychotics in dementia (these increase stroke and death — MHRA)
  • anticholinergics (oxybutynin, tricyclics, sedating antihistamines)
  • long-term PPIs at full dose beyond indication (enteric infection, hypomagnesaemia, B12 deficiency, fracture)
  • NSAIDs with CKD/heart failure or on anticoagulants
  • duplicate drugs from the same class
  • high-dose digoxin in renal impairment
  • and any drug with no evidence-based indication.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.front: Give common START examples (drugs to consider starting).
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.back:
• Anticoagulation in AF (where indicated)
  • statin/ACE inhibitor/beta-blocker/antiplatelet in established cardiovascular disease
  • bone protection (bisphosphonate + calcium/vitamin D) after a fragility fracture
  • ACE inhibitor in heart failure/diabetic nephropathy
  • and inhaled therapy in documented COPD/asthma.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.front: What is the Anticholinergic Burden (ACB) score?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.back: A score that sums the anticholinergic load of every drug in the regimen, including ones not thought of as anticholinergic (amitriptyline and oxybutynin score 3 each; codeine and furosemide score 1 each). A total of 3 or more is the high-burden threshold, linked to delirium, cognitive decline, falls and mortality — a key target for medication review.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.front: What is STOPPFrail?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.back: A set of deprescribing criteria for frail older people with limited life expectancy (e.g. stopping statins/bisphosphonates near end of life, whose long-term benefit won't be realised).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.front: Name other medication-review tools related to STOPP/START.
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.back:
• The Beers Criteria (US equivalent)
  • the Medication Appropriateness Index
  • the '7-Steps' review (NHS Scotland)
  • and multimorbidity guidance (NICE).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.front: Outline the 7-Steps structured medication review.
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.back:
• (1) Aim — what matters to the patient (goals, life expectancy, values)
  • (2) identify essential drugs (don't stop)
  • (3) any unnecessary drugs (no indication/duplication/resolved disease)
  • (4) are therapeutic goals being achieved
  • (5) any safety problem (ADRs, interactions, falls/anticholinergic burden, cascades)
  • (6) cost-effectiveness
  • (7) is the patient willing and able (shared decision, adherence).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.front: What are the key principles of safe deprescribing?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.back:
• Prioritise — start with the drug of greatest harm and least benefit, or the one most likely causing the current problem
  • Shared decision with the patient/carer
  • one change at a time
  • taper drugs that need it (benzodiazepines, opioids, corticosteroids, beta-blockers, some antidepressants) to avoid withdrawal, rebound angina or hypertension, or adrenal insufficiency
  • monitor and document a review plan.
Do not stop anticoagulation in AF for falls risk, or a secondary-prevention statin for age alone.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.front: How should deprescribing be matched to goals of care in advanced frailty/end of life?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.back: Prioritise symptom control and quality of life, and stop drugs with only long-term/preventive benefit (statins, bisphosphonates) whose payoff won't be realised (per STOPPFrail).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.front: What is a pressure ulcer (pressure sore / decubitus ulcer)?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.back: Localised damage to skin and underlying tissue, usually over a bony prominence, caused by sustained pressure — or pressure combined with shear.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.front: Why do pressure ulcers matter?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.back: They are common, largely preventable, painful, costly, and a marker of care quality; in the frail immobile elderly they drive infection, sepsis, prolonged admission and death. Pressure damage arising from omissions in care or neglect is also a safeguarding issue. All pressure ulcers are recorded and reviewed for learning — the older avoidable/unavoidable labelling is no longer used (NHS England).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.front: What is the overarching clinical priority in pressure ulcers?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.back: Prevention over treatment: identify who's at risk, protect the skin relentlessly (the SSKIN bundle), and — if an ulcer develops — grade it, offload it, and manage the wound.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.front: Describe the mechanism of pressure ulcer formation.
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.back: Sustained pressure over a bony prominence → occludes capillaries → local ischaemia → tissue hypoxia and necrosis.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.front: What are the contributing forces in pressure ulcer formation?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.back:
• Pressure (the primary insult)
  • shear (tissue layers slide over each other, e.g. sliding down the bed → deep vessel damage)
  • friction (surface rubbing → superficial breakdown)
  • and moisture (incontinence/sweat macerates skin — moisture-associated damage).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.front: List the common sites of pressure ulcers.
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.back:
Over bony prominences:
  • sacrum
  • heels
  • ischial tuberosities
  • greater trochanters
  • elbows
  • occiput
  • malleoli.
Also device-related (catheters, oxygen tubing, casts, NG tubes).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.front: What is the single biggest risk factor for pressure ulcers?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.back: Immobility (bed/chair-bound, sedation, post-op, paralysis, 'long lie'). Others: reduced sensation, impaired consciousness, malnutrition/dehydration, incontinence/moisture, poor perfusion, older/frail thin skin, and previous pressure ulcer.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.front: How should pressure-ulcer risk be assessed (NICE)?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.back: Assume all patients are potentially at risk; formally assess and document risk in those with risk factors within 6 hours of admission, repeating after any change in condition. Validated tools (Waterlow, Braden, Norton) support but do not replace clinical judgement.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.front: How does early pressure damage differ in darker skin tones?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.back: It may not appear as redness — look for purplish/bluish discolouration, and changes in temperature, firmness, or the patient reporting pain. Palpate, don't just look.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.front: What is a Category 1 pressure ulcer?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.back: Non-blanchable erythema of intact skin (redness that doesn't blanch on pressure; in dark skin, discolouration/temperature change).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.front: What is a Category 2 pressure ulcer?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.back: Partial-thickness skin loss — dermis exposed; a shallow open ulcer or an intact/ruptured blister.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.front: What is a Category 3 pressure ulcer?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.back: Full-thickness skin loss — subcutaneous fat visible; may have slough; but muscle/bone NOT exposed.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.front: What is a Category 4 pressure ulcer?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.back: Full-thickness tissue loss — exposed bone, tendon, or muscle; often slough/eschar, with undermining/tunnelling.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.front: What is an 'unstageable' pressure ulcer?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.back: Full-thickness loss where the base is obscured by slough/eschar, so depth can't be determined until debrided.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.front: What is a 'deep tissue injury'?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.back: Persistent non-blanchable deep red/maroon/purple discolouration or a blood-filled blister, from damage to underlying soft tissue.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.front: What is the SSKIN prevention bundle?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.back:
• Surface (pressure-redistributing mattress/cushion)
  • Skin inspection (regular checks over bony prominences; keep clean/dry)
  • Keep moving (reposition regularly + heel offloading)
  • Incontinence/moisture (manage, barrier creams, keep dry)
  • Nutrition/hydration (screen with MUST, optimise protein/calorie/fluid).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.front: How often should at-risk and high-risk patients be repositioned?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.back: At-risk adults at least every 6 hours; high-risk at least every 4 hours — document the schedule, with heel offloading.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.front: What must you NOT do to skin over bony prominences to prevent ulcers?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.back: Do NOT massage or rub the skin — it causes damage (NICE: do not offer skin massage/rubbing to prevent a pressure ulcer).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.front: What is the first step in managing an established pressure ulcer?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.back: Relieve the pressure — offload immediately (repositioning, appropriate support surface). Nothing heals under continued pressure. Then categorise/document (site, category, size — measure/photograph).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.front: How is debridement approached in pressure ulcers?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.back: Debride slough/necrotic tissue (usually autolytic dressings; sharp or surgical debridement only by a practitioner trained and assessed as competent — tissue viability, or the surgical team for extensive necrosis; larval therapy is an alternative) — BUT a stable dry heel eschar is left intact (protective) unless there is infection or instability.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.front: Which dressings are used for pressure ulcers?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.back: Dressings that maintain a moist wound environment (hydrocolloids, foams, alginates, hydrogels) matched to exudate. Avoid routine gauze (adherent, painful); manage exudate/odour.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.front: How should infection in a pressure ulcer be handled?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.back: Do NOT swab routinely (all ulcers are colonised). Swab/treat only with clinical signs of infection (spreading erythema, heat, increasing pain, systemic upset, cellulitis, delayed healing), taking the sample from the cleansed wound bed rather than the surface. Systemic antibiotics only for spreading infection/cellulitis/osteomyelitis/sepsis — flucloxacillin first-line for surrounding cellulitis (doxycycline or clarithromycin if penicillin-allergic); never topical antibiotics. Suspect osteomyelitis if the ulcer probes to bone or fails to heal — a normal X-ray does not exclude it, MRI is the imaging of choice.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.front: What are the complications of pressure ulcers?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.back:
• Local/systemic infection — cellulitis, osteomyelitis, sepsis
  • chronic non-healing wounds
  • pain
  • fluid/protein loss
  • prolonged admission
  • rarely Marjolin's ulcer (squamous cell carcinoma in a chronic wound)
  • and death.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.front: Why can a pressure ulcer be a safeguarding issue?
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.back: Pressure damage may reflect neglect or omissions in care (missed repositioning, no risk assessment, no support surface), so consider an adult-safeguarding referral and report the ulcer as a patient-safety incident.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.question: Which of the following is one of the five statutory principles of the Mental Capacity Act 2005?
options: Capacity must be positively proven before any treatment is given
Relatives automatically become the decision-maker for an incapacitated adult
The most protective available option should be chosen in every case
An unwise decision does not by itself mean the person lacks capacity
Once capacity has been lost it is presumed to be permanently absent
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.answer: An unwise decision does not by itself mean the person lacks capacity
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.explanation: An UNWISE decision does not equal a lack of capacity — a core MCA principle. Others: capacity is PRESUMED (not proven first); relatives do not automatically decide; the LEAST restrictive option is chosen; capacity is decision- and time-specific, not permanently lost.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.question: A 78-year-old man with mild dementia refuses an operation clinicians recommend. He can explain the operation, its risks and alternatives, remembers the discussion, weighs it up, and communicates a clear 'no'. What is the correct interpretation?
options: He has capacity for this decision and his refusal must be respected
He lacks capacity because he has dementia
He lacks capacity because the decision is unwise
A best-interests decision should override him
His next-of-kin should decide
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.answer: He has capacity for this decision and his refusal must be respected
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.explanation: Capacity is decision-specific and functional: he can understand, retain, weigh and communicate, so he HAS capacity for this decision regardless of a dementia diagnosis or the wisdom of his choice. A capacitous refusal must be respected; best interests and family do not apply while he has capacity.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.question: What are the four abilities assessed in stage 2 (the functional test) of the Mental Capacity Act capacity assessment?
options: Read, write, calculate, and sign
Orientation to time, place, person, and situation
Understand, retain, use/weigh, and communicate the decision
Recall of past medical, drug, and social history
Consent, assent, dissent, and comprehension
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.answer: Understand, retain, use/weigh, and communicate the decision
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.explanation: The MCA functional test asks whether the person can UNDERSTAND the relevant information, RETAIN it, USE OR WEIGH it, and COMMUNICATE their decision. Failure of any one (due to an impairment of mind/brain) means they lack capacity for that decision.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.question: For an Advance Decision to Refuse Treatment (ADRT) to validly refuse life-sustaining treatment, which additional requirement must be met?
options: It must be reviewed and re-signed annually by the person's own GP
It must be approved in advance by the Court of Protection
It must be countersigned by two consultants who know the patient
It must be registered with the Office of the Public Guardian
Written, signed and witnessed, stating it applies even if life is at risk
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.answer: Written, signed and witnessed, stating it applies even if life is at risk
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.explanation: To refuse LIFE-SUSTAINING treatment, an ADRT must be in writing, signed and witnessed, and explicitly state it applies 'even if life is at risk'. Annual review, court approval, consultant countersignature and OPG registration (which applies to LPAs) are not requirements.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.question: Which single statement about an Advance Decision to Refuse Treatment is correct?
options: It can be used to request a specific treatment
A valid, applicable ADRT is legally binding and has the same force as a competent patient's refusal
It can lawfully authorise euthanasia
It can refuse basic care such as warmth and oral food/fluids
It is only advisory and can be overridden in the patient's best interests
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.answer: A valid, applicable ADRT is legally binding and has the same force as a competent patient's refusal
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.explanation: A valid and applicable ADRT is LEGALLY BINDING — the same force as a contemporaneous refusal by a capacitous patient. It can only REFUSE (never demand) treatment, cannot authorise euthanasia (illegal in the UK), and cannot refuse basic care/symptom relief.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.question: Which type of Lasting Power of Attorney allows an attorney to make decisions about medical treatment?
options: Property and Financial Affairs LPA
Enduring Power of Attorney
Either type equally
Health and Welfare LPA
Court of Protection LPA
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.explanation: Only the HEALTH AND WELFARE LPA covers medical treatment, and only once the donor lacks capacity; it covers life-sustaining treatment only if expressly stated. The Property and Financial Affairs LPA covers money/property, not treatment.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.question: A registered Health and Welfare LPA must be registered with which body before it can be used?
options: The Office of the Public Guardian
The Care Quality Commission
The General Medical Council
The Court of Protection
The local safeguarding board
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.answer: The Office of the Public Guardian
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.explanation: An LPA must be registered with the OFFICE OF THE PUBLIC GUARDIAN to be valid. The Court of Protection resolves disputes and can appoint deputies but does not register LPAs; the CQC, GMC and safeguarding boards have other roles.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.question: What is the legal status of an advance statement of wishes and preferences?
options: Legally binding in the same way as an Advance Decision to Refuse Treatment
Binding only where it has been formally signed and independently witnessed
Not legally binding, but must be taken into account in best interests
Binding only where it refuses rather than requests a specific treatment
Of no relevance once the person has lost capacity to make the decision
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.answer: Not legally binding, but must be taken into account in best interests
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.explanation: An advance statement (wishes, values, preferences) is NOT legally binding but MUST be considered when a best-interests decision is made after capacity is lost. It differs from an ADRT (binding refusal) and remains highly relevant, not irrelevant.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.question: A patient made a valid ADRT refusing a treatment, and later (while still capacitous) made a Health and Welfare LPA covering the same treatment. Which document takes precedence?
options: The ADRT, because a refusal of treatment outranks any appointment of an attorney
Neither document is valid once two conflicting instruments exist
Neither applies until the Court of Protection has ruled on which prevails
Whichever of the two the patient's close family consider more appropriate
The later LPA, because the later document takes precedence
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.answer: The later LPA, because the later document takes precedence
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.explanation: Where an ADRT and a Health and Welfare LPA cover the same treatment, the LATER document takes precedence — an LPA made after an ADRT can override it, and an ADRT made after an LPA overrides the attorney. This is why the hierarchy of ADRT over LPA is ordered by date rather than by document type. The family's preference and the court do not decide which applies.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.question: An 82-year-old woman is unconscious after a large stroke. She has a valid, applicable written ADRT (signed, witnessed, stating 'even if life is at risk') refusing mechanical ventilation. Her son insists she would 'want everything done'. What should the team do?
options: Ventilate her, because the family's wishes take priority
Follow the ADRT and not ventilate, as it is legally binding
Apply to the Court of Protection to override the ADRT
Make a best-interests decision ignoring the ADRT
Ventilate her until the LPA can be located
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.answer: Follow the ADRT and not ventilate, as it is legally binding
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.explanation: A valid, applicable ADRT refusing ventilation is legally binding and must be followed — it overrides both best-interests decision-making and the Court of Protection. Family cannot consent or refuse for her (they hold no LPA); their account is evidence, not authority.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.question: An unconscious man lacks capacity, has NO ADRT, NO LPA and NO court-appointed deputy, and needs a decision about serious treatment. His family are contactable. What is the correct process?
options: The family formally consent to the treatment on his behalf
Treatment is withheld until he regains capacity to decide for himself
An IMCA must be appointed before any decision at all can be taken
A best-interests decision by the clinical team, consulting the family
The most senior doctor present decides alone without consulting anyone
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.answer: A best-interests decision by the clinical team, consulting the family
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.explanation: With no ADRT/LPA/deputy, the clinical team makes a BEST-INTERESTS decision, consulting those close to him (who inform but cannot consent) and any advance statement. An IMCA is required only when there is NO ONE to consult; here the family are available, so an IMCA is not mandated.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.question: Regarding a DNACPR decision, which statement is correct?
options: It applies only to cardiopulmonary resuscitation and not to other treatments
It means the patient will receive no active treatment at all
It requires the patient's consent to be valid
It must be authorised by the Court of Protection
It permanently prevents ICU admission
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.answer: It applies only to cardiopulmonary resuscitation and not to other treatments
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.explanation: A DNACPR decision relates ONLY to CPR — all other appropriate treatment (antibiotics, fluids, ICU where indicated) continues. It is a clinical decision that does not require the patient's consent, but there is a legal duty to inform and involve the patient, or those close to them if the patient lacks capacity.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.question: A DNACPR order is placed for a competent patient who is never told or consulted, and there is no reason to think discussion would cause harm. Which legal principle has been breached?
options: The doctrine of double effect in symptom control
The Bolam test of reasonable professional practice
The legal duty to inform and involve the patient in a DNACPR decision
The Gillick competence rule for decision-making by minors
The Bolitho modification requiring logical defensibility
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.answer: The legal duty to inform and involve the patient in a DNACPR decision
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.explanation: There is a legal duty to inform and involve a patient in a DNACPR decision unless doing so would cause them physical or psychological harm — distress alone is not enough. Failing to tell or consult a competent patient without such a reason breaches it. Bolam and Bolitho concern the standard of care in negligence, Gillick concerns decision-making by minors, and double effect concerns proportionate symptom relief.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.question: How does ReSPECT differ from an ADRT?
options: ReSPECT is legally binding whereas an ADRT is only advisory
They are the same document under two different names
ReSPECT can only be completed by the patient, never by a clinician
ReSPECT can authorise assisted dying in an emergency situation
ReSPECT records recommendations and is not itself binding; a valid ADRT is
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.answer: ReSPECT records recommendations and is not itself binding; a valid ADRT is
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.explanation: ReSPECT records recommendations for emergency care and treatment and is not itself legally binding, whereas a valid and applicable ADRT is binding on clinicians. ReSPECT is broader than a DNACPR form, is completed with the patient by a clinician, and can record an existing ADRT — but it does not replace one.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.question: A capacitous 40-year-old Jehovah's Witness refuses a life-saving blood transfusion after major haemorrhage, fully understanding she may die. What is the correct action?
options: Transfuse her in her best interests
Respect her refusal, as a capacitous adult may refuse any treatment even if life-saving
Obtain consent from her next-of-kin
Declare her to lack capacity because the decision is unwise
Apply to court to authorise transfusion
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.answer: Respect her refusal, as a capacitous adult may refuse any treatment even if life-saving
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.explanation: A capacitous adult may refuse ANY treatment, including life-saving treatment, for any or no reason; an unwise decision is not incapacity. Her informed refusal must be respected — best interests, family consent and court applications do not apply while she has capacity.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.question: An attorney under a registered Health and Welfare LPA demands a treatment that the clinical team judges to be futile and not in the patient's interest. What is the correct position?
options: The attorney's demand must be followed as they hold legal authority
The attorney's power falls away as soon as the patient loses capacity
The patient's close family can overrule the attorney's decision
An attorney cannot demand treatment clinicians judge inappropriate
The treatment must be provided pending a ruling from the court
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.answer: An attorney cannot demand treatment clinicians judge inappropriate
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance.explanation: An attorney must act in the donor's BEST INTERESTS and cannot demand treatment that clinicians judge inappropriate/futile, nor consent to something a valid later ADRT refuses. The LPA becomes usable precisely WHEN the donor lacks capacity, so the power is not invalid then.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.question: In benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, what is the underlying mechanism?
options: Endolymphatic hydrops from raised endolymph pressure
Post-viral inflammation of the vestibular nerve
Demyelination of the central vestibular pathways
Otoconia moving freely within a semicircular canal
Ischaemia of the labyrinthine artery territory
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.answer: Otoconia moving freely within a semicircular canal
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.explanation: BPPV is caused by CANALITHIASIS — otoconia (calcium-carbonate crystals) displaced from the utricle into a semicircular canal, moving the endolymph abnormally and signalling false rotation. Endolymphatic hydrops is Meniere's; post-viral nerve inflammation is vestibular neuronitis; demyelination/ischaemia are central causes.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.question: Which semicircular canal is most commonly involved in BPPV?
options: The posterior canal
The anterior (superior) canal
The horizontal (lateral) canal
The posterior canal of the opposite ear
The utricle and saccule
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.explanation: The POSTERIOR canal is involved in about 85–90% of BPPV (its position makes it most likely to collect displaced otoconia). Horizontal-canal BPPV is less common and is diagnosed with the supine roll test; anterior-canal BPPV is rare.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.question: A 72-year-old woman describes brief spinning sensations lasting under a minute whenever she rolls over in bed or looks up to a high shelf. She has no hearing loss or tinnitus and is well between episodes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Meniere's disease
Vestibular neuronitis
Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
Posterior-circulation stroke
Vestibular migraine
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.explanation: The triad of a positional trigger, very brief episodes (seconds), and NO hearing loss/tinnitus is classic BPPV. Meniere's has hearing loss/tinnitus/fullness; vestibular neuronitis is constant and prolonged; stroke gives persistent vertigo with neuro signs; vestibular migraine has headache/migraine features.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.question: Which test is the gold-standard for diagnosing posterior-canal BPPV?
options: The supine roll test
The Epley manoeuvre
The head impulse test in isolation
Pure-tone audiometry
The Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.explanation: The DIX-HALLPIKE manoeuvre is diagnostic for posterior-canal BPPV ('D for Diagnosis'). The supine roll test is for horizontal-canal BPPV; the Epley manoeuvre is the TREATMENT; the head impulse test is one component of HINTS; audiometry assesses hearing (normal in BPPV).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.question: During a Dix-Hallpike test, which finding indicates a positive result consistent with BPPV rather than a central cause?
options: Immediate, sustained vertical nystagmus with no latency at all
Upbeating torsional nystagmus after a latency, which fatigues
Direction-changing nystagmus that persists and does not fatigue
Nystagmus present only when the eyes are closed behind lenses
No nystagmus at all, but severe and persistent occipital headache
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.answer: Upbeating torsional nystagmus after a latency, which fatigues
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.explanation: A positive Dix-Hallpike shows, after a brief LATENCY, upbeating torsional nystagmus with the upper pole beating toward the affected (lower) ear, with reproduced vertigo, settling within a minute and FATIGABLE on repeat. Immediate, non-fatiguing, vertical or direction-changing nystagmus suggests a CENTRAL cause and warrants imaging.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.question: A patient has a positive Dix-Hallpike test confirming right posterior-canal BPPV. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
options: Long-term prochlorperazine
Betahistine and a low-salt diet
Urgent MRI brain
The Epley (canalith repositioning) manoeuvre
Vestibular nerve section
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.explanation: First-line treatment for confirmed posterior-canal BPPV is the EPLEY manoeuvre, which repositions the otoconia back into the utricle and is often curative. Vestibular sedatives are not recommended; betahistine/low-salt is for Meniere's; MRI and surgery are reserved for atypical/central or intractable cases.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.question: A 68-year-old man is prescribed regular prochlorperazine for several weeks for typical BPPV, with little improvement. What is the problem with this management?
options: Vestibular sedatives have no role in BPPV and delay compensation
The prochlorperazine dose is too low for an elderly patient
He should have betahistine added alongside the prochlorperazine
Prochlorperazine should have been given intravenously instead
He needs a course of antibiotics for presumed labyrinthitis
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.answer: Vestibular sedatives have no role in BPPV and delay compensation
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.explanation: Vestibular sedatives have no useful role in BPPV: each attack lasts under a minute, they do not address the mechanical cause, and they DELAY central compensation. The effective treatment is a canalith repositioning (Epley) manoeuvre. In an older patient the harm is not just inaction — prochlorperazine causes sedation, postural hypotension, confusion and drug-induced parkinsonism, all of which raise falls risk, and prolonged use risks tardive dyskinesia. (Short-term prochlorperazine is appropriate in vestibular neuronitis, not BPPV.)

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.question: A 70-year-old presents with sudden, persistent vertigo that does not stop when still, vertical nystagmus, and difficulty walking unaided. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Perform the Epley manoeuvre and discharge him home
Reassure and treat as benign positional vertigo
Assess for a central cause and arrange urgent imaging
Start betahistine for presumed Meniere's disease
Prescribe cinnarizine and review him in six weeks
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.answer: Assess for a central cause and arrange urgent imaging
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.explanation: Persistent (non-positional) vertigo, VERTICAL nystagmus and inability to walk are central red flags pointing to a posterior-circulation stroke. This is acute vestibular syndrome, where HINTS is the appropriate bedside examination and urgent imaging is needed — not bedside repositioning or vestibular sedatives. HINTS has no role in episodic positional vertigo.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.question: A 55-year-old woman has recurrent vertigo lasting hours, with a roaring tinnitus, fluctuating hearing loss, and a sensation of fullness in one ear. Which diagnosis does this fit, distinguishing it from BPPV?
options: BPPV
Vestibular neuronitis
Acoustic neuroma
Posterior-circulation stroke
Meniere's disease
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.explanation: Vertigo lasting hours WITH hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness is MENIERE'S disease (endolymphatic hydrops) — the presence of cochlear symptoms and longer duration separate it from BPPV, which is brief, positional, and has no hearing loss/tinnitus.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.question: What is the approximate duration of a single BPPV vertigo episode?
options: 5–10 minutes
A few seconds up to about a minute
Several hours
Constant for days
Only while asleep
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.answer: A few seconds up to about a minute
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.explanation: BPPV episodes are very brief — typically about 20–60 seconds — and settle when the head is kept still. Episodes lasting hours suggest Meniere's; constant vertigo for days suggests vestibular neuronitis or a central cause.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.question: Which is the single commonest cause of vertigo?
options: Meniere's disease
Vestibular neuronitis
Vestibular migraine
Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
Posterior-circulation stroke
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.explanation: BPPV is the single commonest cause of vertigo. It is also an important, treatable contributor to falls in older adults.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.question: A patient successfully treated with the Epley manoeuvre asks about the future. What is the most accurate counselling regarding recurrence?
options: Recurrence is common and the manoeuvre can simply be repeated
Once treated with the Epley, BPPV does not come back
Recurrence usually indicates an underlying central cause
Recurrence means the Epley manoeuvre was performed incorrectly
Lifelong vestibular sedatives are needed to prevent recurrence
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.answer: Recurrence is common and the manoeuvre can simply be repeated
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.explanation: BPPV recurs in roughly half of patients over the following years; the Epley manoeuvre can simply be repeated. Recurrence does not imply sinister pathology or incorrect technique, and long-term vestibular sedatives are not indicated — in older people they add sedation, postural hypotension and falls risk.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.question: A patient has vertigo provoked by rolling side to side while lying flat, and the Dix-Hallpike is unremarkable. Which test should be performed to look for a less common form of BPPV?
options: Pure-tone audiometry
Romberg's test
The supine roll (head-turn) test
Fukuda stepping test
Caloric testing only
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.explanation: Horizontal (lateral) canal BPPV is diagnosed with the SUPINE ROLL test, not the Dix-Hallpike. It is less common than posterior-canal BPPV but should be considered when the history is positional but Dix-Hallpike is negative.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.question: Which statement about imaging in typical BPPV is correct?
options: A CT head is mandatory before any repositioning manoeuvre
MRI is required in every case to confirm canalithiasis
Carotid Doppler ultrasound is the first-line investigation
A skull X-ray demonstrates the displaced otoconia
No imaging in typical BPPV; MRI only if atypical or central
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.answer: No imaging in typical BPPV; MRI only if atypical or central
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.explanation: Typical BPPV is a clinical/bedside diagnosis (positive Dix-Hallpike) and needs NO imaging. MRI is reserved for atypical presentations or central red flags. Canalithiasis is not visible on routine imaging.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.question: Following which condition can BPPV develop as a recognised association?
options: Otosclerosis affecting the stapes footplate
Vestibular neuronitis or labyrinthitis
Presbycusis with high-frequency hearing loss
Chronic otitis media with a persistent effusion
Surgical resection of an acoustic neuroma
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign P.explanation: BPPV is often idiopathic but is recognised after head trauma, with ageing, after prolonged bed rest, and FOLLOWING vestibular neuronitis/labyrinthitis. The other conditions are not the classic antecedents of BPPV.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.question: Which statement best describes comprehensive geriatric assessment (CGA)?
options: A single validated frailty score
A screening blood-test panel for older adults
A one-off assessment performed by the admitting doctor alone
A multidimensional, multidisciplinary process producing a coordinated care plan
A questionnaire completed by the patient at home
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.answer: A multidimensional, multidisciplinary process producing a coordinated care plan
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.explanation: CGA is a multidimensional (several domains) and multidisciplinary (team-delivered) PROCESS that yields a coordinated, patient-centred management plan reviewed iteratively. It is not a score, a blood panel, a single-clinician clerking, or a self-completed questionnaire.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.question: Which of the following is one of the domains assessed in CGA?
options: Functional status — ADLs, IADLs and mobility
Genomic risk profiling for late-onset disease
Radiological staging of comorbid malignancy
Occupational pension entitlement calculation
Formal driving-licence fitness certification
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.answer: Functional status — ADLs, IADLs and mobility
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.explanation: CGA domains are physical/medical, psychological, FUNCTIONAL (ADLs/IADLs, mobility), social, environmental, and future wishes. The other options are not CGA domains.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.question: An 86-year-old woman is admitted after recurrent falls. She has dementia, takes 11 medications, is incontinent, and her daughter (main carer) is exhausted. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: A single-organ cardiology work-up only
Discharge once the acute issue is treated, with no further review
Comprehensive geriatric assessment with the multidisciplinary team
Referral to a single specialist for the falls alone
Commence long-term bed rest for safety
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.answer: Comprehensive geriatric assessment with the multidisciplinary team
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.explanation: This frail, multimorbid patient with falls, cognitive impairment, polypharmacy, incontinence and carer strain is the ideal candidate for CGA — a multidimensional, MDT process addressing all these problems together. A single-organ work-up or isolated referral would miss the interacting issues; bed rest causes deconditioning.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.question: The strongest evidence for CGA improving outcomes (being alive and in one's own home, with less institutionalisation) comes from which setting?
options: Routine outpatient clinics attended by fit older adults
Community pharmacy medication reviews for over-65s
Elective pre-operative assessment clinics before day surgery
Population-wide screening of everyone over the age of 65
Emergency admission of frail older people to geriatric wards
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.answer: Emergency admission of frail older people to geriatric wards
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.explanation: The strongest trial evidence is for CGA in frail older people admitted as an EMERGENCY to inpatient geriatric care: they are more likely to be alive and living in their own home at follow-up and less likely to be institutionalised. The benefit is not established for routine outpatient, community-pharmacy or population-screening settings.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.question: Which tool is most appropriate for assessing the FUNCTIONAL domain (basic activities of daily living) in CGA?
options: The 4AT
The Barthel Index
The Geriatric Depression Scale
STOPP/START criteria
The MUST score
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.explanation: The Barthel Index assesses basic ADLs (function). The 4AT screens for delirium (psychological), the Geriatric Depression Scale for mood, STOPP/START for medication appropriateness, and MUST for nutrition.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.question: Which tool is used within CGA specifically to screen for delirium?
options: Barthel Index
Timed Up-and-Go
MUST
4AT
PRISMA-7
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.explanation: The 4AT is a rapid delirium screening tool (part of the psychological/cognitive domain). Barthel and Timed Up-and-Go assess function/mobility, MUST assesses nutrition, and PRISMA-7 is a frailty-identification tool.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.question: Which activity is an instrumental activity of daily living (IADL) rather than a basic ADL?
options: Managing finances and medications
Dressing
Feeding oneself
Transferring from bed to chair
Toileting
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.explanation: IADLs are more complex independent-living tasks such as managing finances/medications, shopping, cooking and using transport. Dressing, feeding, transfers and toileting are basic ADLs (self-care).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.question: Which member of the CGA multidisciplinary team is best placed to assess the home environment, falls hazards, and aids/adaptations?
options: Pharmacist
Dietitian
Occupational therapist
Speech and language therapist
Phlebotomist
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.explanation: The occupational therapist assesses function/ADLs and performs the home/environmental assessment, recommending aids and adaptations. The pharmacist reviews medication, the dietitian nutrition, and SALT swallow/communication.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.question: What is the correct FIRST step of the CGA process?
options: Write the discharge summary and the GP letter
Hold the multidisciplinary team meeting first
Complete a full drug chart reconciliation
Arrange the follow-up appointment in advance
Identify the right patients using a frailty screen
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.answer: Identify the right patients using a frailty screen
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.explanation: CGA begins by IDENTIFYING the patients who will benefit — older people with frailty/multimorbidity, screened with a tool such as the Clinical Frailty Scale, PRISMA-7 or gait speed. Assessment, MDT synthesis, planning, and review/follow-up come afterwards.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.question: A 68-year-old who lives alone, drives, walks his dog daily and takes one regular medicine is admitted with an isolated ankle fracture. Is full comprehensive geriatric assessment specifically indicated?
options: Yes — every patient admitted over the age of 65
No — CGA is targeted at frail, multimorbid older people
Yes — because he has reached retirement age
No — CGA is only used after a hip fracture
Yes — CGA is required before any fracture is treated
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.answer: No — CGA is targeted at frail, multimorbid older people
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.explanation: CGA is TARGETED at those who benefit most — frail, multimorbid older people — not every older patient. A fit, independent person with a single problem does not specifically require the full CGA process (though good care still applies).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.question: Which cluster represents the 'geriatric giants' / frailty syndromes that CGA is designed to surface?
options: Hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, diabetes, obesity and smoking
Asthma, COPD, bronchiectasis, pulmonary fibrosis and sleep apnoea
Anaemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, myeloma and lymphoma
Falls, immobility, delirium, incontinence and iatrogenic harm
Cataract, glaucoma, macular degeneration, dry eye and blepharitis
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.answer: Falls, immobility, delirium, incontinence and iatrogenic harm
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.explanation: The geriatric giants/frailty syndromes are falls, immobility, delirium/confusion, incontinence, and iatrogenic harm (polypharmacy). CGA is structured precisely to detect and manage these often-missed, interacting problems.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.question: A frail 82-year-old is listed for major elective colorectal surgery. Which service model is designed to deliver CGA in this situation?
options: Perioperative CGA by an older-people's surgical liaison team
Routine pre-assessment clinic nurse questionnaire alone
Post-operative acute pain service review on the ward
Standard post-operative physiotherapy referral
Palliative care outpatient support after discharge
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.answer: Perioperative CGA by an older-people's surgical liaison team
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.explanation: Perioperative CGA — delivered by an older-people's surgical liaison service, often called POPS — brings comprehensive geriatric assessment to frail patients before and after major surgery, optimising medical problems, medication, nutrition and function, and setting realistic goals. It is associated with fewer post-operative complications and shorter stays than standard pre-assessment alone.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.question: Why is urgent 'front-door' CGA in the emergency department or same-day emergency care valued?
options: It ensures every frail patient is admitted for observation
It removes the need for a separate medication review
It avoids unnecessary admission and the harm of bed rest
It removes the need for any formal frailty score
It shortens waiting times for urgent radiology
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.answer: It avoids unnecessary admission and the harm of bed rest
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.explanation: Rapid CGA at the front door can prevent unnecessary admissions and the DECONDITIONING that results from bed rest, supporting safe discharge or admission-avoidance. It does not guarantee admission and is not merely an administrative step.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.question: Within CGA, which criteria set is used to guide medication review and reduce inappropriate polypharmacy?
options: CHA2DS2-VASc
GRACE score
Wells score
CURB-65
STOPP/START
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehe.explanation: STOPP/START criteria guide the pharmacist-led medication review in CGA (STOPP = potentially inappropriate medications to stop; START = beneficial medications being omitted). The others are stroke/bleeding/VTE/pneumonia risk scores unrelated to polypharmacy review.
