options: Resuscitation is futile below 30degC and should be stopped
Confirm death immediately if there is no pulse
Only warm the limbs
Give three doses of adrenaline immediately
'No one is dead until warm and dead' - continue CPR through rewarming
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.answer: 'No one is dead until warm and dead' - continue CPR through rewarming
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.explanation: 'No one is dead until warm and dead' - the cold brain tolerates arrest far longer, so CPR is continued through rewarming and death is confirmed only after rewarming. Consider extracorporeal (ECMO) rewarming for arrested/refractory cases.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.question: Which rewarming method is most appropriate for MILD hypothermia (32–35degC)?
options: Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation
Passive external rewarming (remove wet clothes, blankets, warm room)
Peritoneal lavage
Warm packs to the hands and feet
Immediate cardiopulmonary bypass
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.answer: Passive external rewarming (remove wet clothes, blankets, warm room)
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.explanation: Mild hypothermia is managed with PASSIVE EXTERNAL rewarming - removing wet clothing, blankets and a warm environment (aiming ~0.5–2degC/hour). Active external (e.g. forced warm air) is for moderate, and active internal/ECMO for severe/arrested cases.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.question: An elderly man's core temperature is 26degC and he appears dead with fixed dilated pupils and a potassium of 13 mmol/L. What do these findings indicate?
options: Death can be confirmed now, as this potassium is incompatible with life
Death can be confirmed on the fixed dilated pupils alone
The potassium should be corrected before any decision is made
Pupils are unreliable when cold; a potassium this high predicts a poor outcome
He should be rewarmed and resuscitated whatever the potassium shows
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.answer: Pupils are unreliable when cold; a potassium this high predicts a poor outcome
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.explanation: In hypothermia, fixed dilated pupils and apparent rigidity are NOT reliable signs of death, so death is confirmed only after rewarming. A markedly raised potassium (around 12 mmol/L or above) carries a very poor outcome and is one factor a specialist team weighs when deciding about extracorporeal rewarming or stopping — it is never used alone, and the decision is a senior one.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.question: A hypothermic patient is found to have removed most of their clothing despite the cold. What is this recognised phenomenon called?
options: Paradoxical undressing
Cold diuresis
Afterdrop
The lucid interval
Terminal burrowing only
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.answer: Paradoxical undressing
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.explanation: 'Paradoxical undressing' - removing clothes due to a confused sensation of warmth - is a recognised feature of severe hypothermia.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.question: Which underlying causes should be actively considered and treated in an elderly patient with hypothermia?
options: Hyperthyroidism and hyperglycaemia
Asthma and eczema
Hypothyroidism, hypoglycaemia and sepsis
Migraine and epilepsy
Gout and pseudogout
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.answer: Hypothyroidism, hypoglycaemia and sepsis
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.explanation: Reduced heat production from HYPOTHYROIDISM, HYPOGLYCAEMIA and SEPSIS (which can cause hypothermia rather than fever in the elderly) should be sought and treated, along with environmental exposure and alcohol. TFTs, glucose and cultures are part of the work-up.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.question: Which fluid management is appropriate in hypothermia, and why?
options: Fluid restriction, because the patient is oedematous
Cold IV fluids to match body temperature
No fluids until the patient is fully rewarmed
Rapid cold saline boluses
Warmed IV fluids, because cold diuresis causes hypovolaemia
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.answer: Warmed IV fluids, because cold diuresis causes hypovolaemia
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthe.explanation: Cold diuresis causes hypovolaemia, so WARMED IV fluids are given (also contributing to core rewarming). Cold fluids would worsen hypothermia, and withholding fluids ignores the volume depletion.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.question: Which is the validated UK tool for screening for malnutrition, and what does it assess?
options: The Glasgow Coma Scale, which assesses conscious level
CURB-65, which assesses the severity of pneumonia
The Barthel Index, which assesses activities of daily living
MUST — BMI, unplanned weight loss, and acute disease effect
FRAX, which estimates ten-year fragility fracture risk
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.answer: MUST — BMI, unplanned weight loss, and acute disease effect
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.explanation: The Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool (MUST) scores BMI, unplanned weight loss over 3–6 months, and an acute disease effect (no intake >5 days), giving low/medium/high risk categories. The others assess consciousness, pneumonia, function and fracture risk.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.question: A patient's MUST score is 3. How is this interpreted and managed?
options: High risk - refer to dietitian and start a nutrition support plan
Low risk - routine rescreen only
Medium risk - food diary only
Normal - no action
It indicates refeeding syndrome is present
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.answer: High risk - refer to dietitian and start a nutrition support plan
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.explanation: A MUST score of ≥2 is HIGH risk, warranting treatment - dietitian referral and a nutrition support plan. A score of 0 is low risk (rescreen) and 1 is medium risk (observe/food diary). The score itself does not diagnose refeeding syndrome.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.question: A malnourished older man has a low serum albumin. How should this be interpreted?
options: It confirms the diagnosis and severity of malnutrition
It excludes malnutrition
Albumin is a marker of illness/inflammation, not a reliable nutritional marker
It indicates refeeding syndrome
It is the target of nutritional treatment
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.answer: Albumin is a marker of illness/inflammation, not a reliable nutritional marker
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.explanation: Albumin reflects illness and inflammation, NOT nutritional status, and is not a reliable nutritional marker. Malnutrition is identified by screening (MUST), weight/intake history and clinical assessment - not by albumin.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.question: What is the correct FIRST-LINE ('food first') management for an older person identified as malnourished?
options: Start oral nutritional supplements before any dietary change
Insert a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy tube
Begin parenteral nutrition through a central line
Restrict intake initially to avoid refeeding syndrome
Food fortification, energy-dense meals, and addressing barriers
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.answer: Food fortification, energy-dense meals, and addressing barriers
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.explanation: 'Food first' is the foundation: fortify food (cream, butter, cheese, milk powder, oils), give small frequent energy-dense meals and nourishing snacks/drinks, and address barriers (dentition, dysphagia, assistance, mood, drugs). ONS, enteral and parenteral feeding are escalations if food-first is insufficient.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.question: When should oral nutritional supplements (ONS) be prescribed?
options: Routinely for every older patient at hospital admission
When food-first measures alone do not meet requirements
Before any attempt at dietary change or fortification
Only in patients who already have a feeding tube in place
Only where the gastrointestinal tract is non-functional
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.answer: When food-first measures alone do not meet requirements
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.explanation: Food-first measures come first and continue alongside, but ONS are indicated when food alone does not meet requirements. In someone at high risk or already malnourished they are started together with dietary advice rather than held back until food-first has demonstrably failed. They are prescribed against ACBS indications, with a defined goal, and reviewed and stopped as intake recovers.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.question: An 84-year-old woman with advanced dementia is no longer eating well, and her family ask about a feeding tube (PEG). What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Insert a PEG, as tube feeding improves survival in advanced dementia
Start parenteral nutrition until her oral intake recovers
Withhold all food and fluids, as she is at the end of life
Tube feeding is not recommended; comfort hand feeding is preferred
Place a nasogastric tube immediately and feed overnight
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.answer: Tube feeding is not recommended; comfort hand feeding is preferred
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.explanation: In advanced dementia, tube feeding does NOT improve outcomes and is generally not recommended - it is a best-interests/ethical decision, and comfort/hand feeding is preferred. PEG/NG/parenteral feeding would not benefit her and carry risks.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.question: What is the underlying mechanism of refeeding syndrome?
options: Carbohydrate triggers an insulin surge, driving phosphate into cells
Insulin deficiency causing hyperglycaemia and an osmotic diuresis
Excess dietary protein causing a rising urea and encephalopathy
Acute vitamin C deficiency impairing collagen and vessel integrity
Sodium overload causing hypertension and pulmonary oedema
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.answer: Carbohydrate triggers an insulin surge, driving phosphate into cells
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.explanation: In refeeding syndrome, giving carbohydrate to a starved patient triggers an INSULIN SURGE that drives phosphate, potassium, magnesium and glucose into cells (with thiamine consumption), causing dangerous drops in serum phosphate/potassium/magnesium and fluid shifts - leading to arrhythmias, cardiac/respiratory failure, seizures and Wernicke's.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.question: What is the biochemical hallmark of refeeding syndrome?
options: Hyperkalaemia
Hypercalcaemia
Hypophosphataemia
Hypernatraemia
Hyperglycaemia
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.explanation: Hypophosphataemia is the hallmark of refeeding syndrome (with falls in potassium and magnesium too). Phosphate, potassium and magnesium must be monitored and replaced daily during refeeding.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.question: Which of the following, on its own, makes a patient HIGH risk for refeeding syndrome by NICE criteria?
options: A BMI of 17 with no other risk factors present
Unintentional weight loss of 8% over the last four months
Little or no nutritional intake for the past six days
A history of alcohol misuse with otherwise normal bloods
A BMI below 16
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.explanation: BMI below 16 is one of the single high-risk criteria, alongside unintentional weight loss above 15% in 3–6 months, little or no intake for more than 10 days, and low potassium, phosphate or magnesium before feeding. A BMI of 17, an 8% loss, six days without intake and an alcohol history each sit in the 'two or more' list — any one of them alone is not sufficient (NICE).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.question: A severely malnourished patient at high refeeding risk is about to start feeding. What is the correct approach?
options: Feed at full estimated requirements immediately to correct the deficit
Start low and slow at a maximum of about 10 kcal/kg/day, with thiamine first
Give a large intravenous glucose bolus before starting any feed
Withhold all vitamins until the electrolytes have fully normalised
Start parenteral nutrition at the full rate through a central line
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.answer: Start low and slow at a maximum of about 10 kcal/kg/day, with thiamine first
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.explanation: To prevent refeeding syndrome, feeding is started LOW and SLOW (max ~10 kcal/kg/day, 5 in extreme cases), thiamine and B-complex/multivitamins are given BEFORE and during feeding (to prevent Wernicke's), and phosphate/potassium/magnesium are monitored and replaced daily. Rapid full feeding or a glucose bolus would precipitate the syndrome.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.question: A frail 82-year-old has lost weight, her rings and dentures are loose, and she has temporal muscle wasting. What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Start parenteral nutrition immediately through a central line
Reassure her that weight loss is a normal part of ageing
Prescribe an appetite stimulant as the first-line intervention
Screen with MUST, find the cause, and begin food-first measures
Arrange a PEG tube to secure her nutritional intake
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.answer: Screen with MUST, find the cause, and begin food-first measures
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.explanation: The first step is to screen formally (MUST), identify the underlying cause, and begin food-first measures — fortification, energy-dense meals and snacks, and addressing barriers to eating. Screening and food-first run in parallel with a red-flag review: unexplained weight loss in an older person still needs a suspected-cancer pathway referral where red flags are present, and must not simply be attributed to ageing.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.question: A 78-year-old is four days into a large left hemisphere stroke. A swallow assessment finds she cannot swallow safely and she is eating and drinking nothing. Her abdomen is soft with normal bowel sounds. Which feeding route is most appropriate?
options: Enteral tube feeding (NG initially, PEG if long-term)
Continue oral feeding regardless
Parenteral nutrition
Food fortification alone
No nutrition until swallow recovers
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.answer: Enteral tube feeding (NG initially, PEG if long-term)
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.explanation: When the gut works but oral intake is unsafe (e.g. stroke dysphagia), ENTERAL tube feeding is appropriate - NG initially, and PEG if long-term. Parenteral nutrition is reserved for a non-functioning/inaccessible gut, and continuing oral feeding risks aspiration.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.question: A chronically undernourished patient with a history of alcohol misuse is being started on nutrition. Which vitamin must be given before and during feeding to prevent a serious complication?
options: Vitamin C
Vitamin K
Thiamine (vitamin B1)
Vitamin D
Folate alone
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.explanation: Thiamine (B1) must be given before and during refeeding (with B-complex/multivitamins) to prevent Wernicke's encephalopathy, as refeeding consumes thiamine - especially important given the alcohol history.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.question: Parenteral nutrition is appropriate in which situation?
options: When a patient with dysphagia after stroke cannot swallow safely
When a patient repeatedly refuses oral nutritional supplements
When serum albumin stays low despite adequate oral intake
When enteral feeding is causing troublesome diarrhoea
Only when the gastrointestinal tract is non-functional or inaccessible
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.answer: Only when the gastrointestinal tract is non-functional or inaccessible
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutri.explanation: Parenteral nutrition is reserved for a NON-FUNCTIONING or inaccessible GI tract (obstruction, short bowel, ileus) and carries infection/line risks. Where the gut works, oral (food first/ONS) or enteral routes are preferred.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.question: Why does a DISPLACED intracapsular neck of femur fracture usually require joint replacement rather than internal fixation?
options: Because the femoral neck bone is too osteoporotic to hold a screw
Because internal fixation is technically impossible at this site
Because joint replacement is a cheaper operation than fixation
Because the retrograde blood supply to the femoral head is disrupted
Because a displaced fracture cannot be reduced closed in an older patient
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.answer: Because the retrograde blood supply to the femoral head is disrupted
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.explanation: Intracapsular fractures disrupt the RETROGRADE blood supply to the femoral head, so a displaced intracapsular fracture has a high risk of avascular necrosis and non-union if fixed - hence the head is replaced (total hip replacement or hemiarthroplasty).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.question: A 74-year-old normally walks to the shops with a stick, lives alone and manages all his own care, with no significant comorbidity. He has a displaced intracapsular hip fracture. Which operation is preferred?
options: Total hip replacement
Dynamic hip screw
Intramedullary nail
Hemiarthroplasty
Cannulated screws (internal fixation)
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.explanation: For a displaced intracapsular fracture, TOTAL HIP REPLACEMENT is favoured over hemiarthroplasty when the patient walked independently outdoors with no more than a stick, has no comorbidity making the procedure unsuitable, and is expected to be independent in activities of daily living beyond 2 years (NICE). This independently mobile, medically fit 74-year-old meets those criteria.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.question: A frail 90-year-old with dementia who mobilises only indoors with a frame has a displaced intracapsular hip fracture. Which operation is most appropriate?
options: Total hip replacement
Dynamic hip screw
Hemiarthroplasty
Intramedullary nail
Internal fixation with screws
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.explanation: A displaced intracapsular fracture needs joint replacement. This patient mobilises only indoors with a frame and is not expected to be independent in activities of daily living beyond 2 years, so HEMIARTHROPLASTY is preferred. Note that dementia alone is not an automatic bar to total hip replacement (NICE) — it is one comorbidity to weigh; here it is the pre-fracture mobility and expected function that decide.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.question: A stable inter-trochanteric (extracapsular) hip fracture is best treated with which implant?
options: Total hip replacement
Hemiarthroplasty
Cannulated screws
Conservative traction only
Dynamic hip screw (DHS)
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.explanation: A stable inter-trochanteric EXTRACAPSULAR fracture is fixed with a dynamic hip screw (DHS). Extracapsular fractures leave the femoral head blood supply intact, so fixation (not replacement) is appropriate. Sub-trochanteric/reverse-oblique patterns are nailed.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.question: A sub-trochanteric (reverse-oblique) femoral fracture is best managed with which device?
options: Dynamic hip screw
Intramedullary nail
Hemiarthroplasty
Total hip replacement
Plaster cast
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.explanation: Sub-trochanteric and reverse-oblique/transverse extracapsular fractures are managed with an INTRAMEDULLARY NAIL (a DHS is used for stable inter-trochanteric patterns).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.question: Within what timeframe should surgery ideally be performed for a hip fracture, per NICE?
options: Within 6 hours
Within 1 week
Only after 48 hours of optimisation
On the day of, or day after, admission (within ~36 hours)
Whenever a list is free, regardless of delay
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.answer: On the day of, or day after, admission (within ~36 hours)
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.explanation: NICE recommends surgery on the day of, or the day after, admission - within ~36 hours - on a planned trauma list. This is the single most important peri-operative target; delay worsens mortality, delirium and pressure sores.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.question: Which is an ACCEPTABLE reason to delay hip-fracture surgery for medical optimisation?
options: Uncontrolled heart failure or a significant electrolyte abnormality
That the patient has presented outside normal working hours
That the patient is on a stable long-term dose of a statin
A minor derangement that cannot be corrected before surgery
That the patient is over the age of 85 with several comorbidities
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.answer: Uncontrolled heart failure or a significant electrolyte abnormality
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.explanation: Acceptable (correctable) reasons to delay include severe anaemia, uncontrolled heart failure, significant electrolyte/coagulation abnormality, uncontrolled diabetes, or a chest infection needing treatment. Being out of hours, minor/uncorrectable derangements, or age are NOT acceptable reasons to delay.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.question: An 82-year-old with a hip fracture is in severe pain. What is the most appropriate analgesic approach?
options: High-dose opioids alone, avoiding paracetamol to reduce the tablet burden
An oral NSAID first-line, with paracetamol added if needed
Regular paracetamol with an opioid, adding a block to limit the opioid dose
Regular paracetamol alone, avoiding all opioids because of delirium risk
Withhold analgesia until the fascia iliaca block can be sited in theatre
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.answer: Regular paracetamol with an opioid, adding a block to limit the opioid dose
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.explanation: The NICE ladder is regular paracetamol 6-hourly, adding an immediate-release opioid if that is not enough, then a fascia iliaca compartment block if paracetamol plus an opioid is still insufficient or to limit the opioid dose — blocks reduce delirium, respiratory depression and constipation. Opioids are offered, not withheld; NSAIDs are not used in hip fracture; and a block is never a substitute for early surgery.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.question: Which statement about anaesthesia for hip-fracture surgery is correct?
options: Spinal anaesthesia is superior to general for survival and recovery
General anaesthesia is contraindicated in patients over the age of 80
Surgery should be done under local infiltration wherever possible
A regional nerve block removes the need for any formal anaesthetic
Either spinal or general is acceptable, with no clear superiority
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.answer: Either spinal or general is acceptable, with no clear superiority
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.explanation: Evidence shows NO clear superiority of spinal over general anaesthesia for survival or recovery - either is acceptable. The belief that spinal is always better is a common misconception.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.question: A hip-fracture patient is admitted. Beyond the orthopaedic fixation, which model of care improves mortality and length of stay?
options: Care by the orthopaedic team alone, with medical referral if needed
Orthogeriatric shared care with geriatric assessment within 72 hours
Discharge planning begun only after two weeks of protected bed rest
Care led by the physiotherapy team with medical input as required
Early discharge with outpatient orthopaedic and medical follow-up
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.answer: Orthogeriatric shared care with geriatric assessment within 72 hours
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.explanation: Formal ORTHOGERIATRIC shared care - joint management by orthopaedics and geriatrics with comprehensive geriatric assessment within 72 hours - reduces mortality, length of stay and complications. It is the model of integrated care for hip fracture.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.question: When should a patient be mobilised after hip-fracture surgery?
options: Strict bed rest for one week
Only once the wound has fully healed
After 72 hours of traction
The day after surgery, then at least daily
Only if pain-free without analgesia
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.answer: The day after surgery, then at least daily
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.explanation: Patients should be mobilised the DAY AFTER surgery (with physiotherapy) and then at least daily. Surgery aims to permit immediate full weight-bearing; early mobilisation prevents deconditioning, VTE, pneumonia and pressure sores.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.question: A patient recovers from hip-fracture surgery. Which secondary prevention must not be missed?
options: Bone protection plus a multifactorial falls assessment
No further action once the fracture has been surgically fixed
A DEXA scan at six months, deferring treatment until the result
A period of bed rest to allow the fracture to consolidate
Long-term prophylactic antibiotics to protect the implant
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.answer: Bone protection plus a multifactorial falls assessment
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.explanation: A fragility hip fracture IS the diagnosis of osteoporosis, so bone protection is started before discharge — vitamin D (with calcium only if dietary intake is inadequate) plus a bisphosphonate, without waiting for a DEXA scan. And because a hip fracture is 'a fall until proven otherwise', a multifactorial falls assessment must be done to prevent recurrence.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.question: On examination, which finding suggests a neck of femur fracture?
options: A lengthened, internally rotated leg with a palpable femoral head
Bilateral pitting oedema to the knees with a normal hip examination
Shortened, externally rotated leg; Shenton's line disrupted
A flexed, adducted and internally rotated leg held off the bed
Foot drop with loss of sensation over the dorsum of the foot
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.answer: Shortened, externally rotated leg; Shenton's line disrupted
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.explanation: A hip fracture classically produces a SHORTENED, EXTERNALLY ROTATED leg, with a disrupted Shenton's line on X-ray. If the X-ray is normal but fracture is suspected, MRI (or CT) is used to detect an occult fracture.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.question: An older patient presents having fallen and fractured their hip; they are also febrile and hypotensive. What is an important principle of pre-operative care?
options: Proceed straight to theatre, since delay worsens hip-fracture mortality
Delay surgery until the fever has fully settled, however long that takes
Treat the fever as incidental, since a fracture explains the presentation
Give a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory for both the pain and the fever
Resuscitate (A-E) and treat the cause of the fall
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.answer: Resuscitate (A-E) and treat the cause of the fall
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of.explanation: A fall causing a hip fracture may be the presentation of acute illness (sepsis, MI, arrhythmia, stroke, delirium). Pre-operative care includes A-E resuscitation and treating the underlying cause - while still aiming to operate within ~36 hours and not delaying for minor/uncorrectable issues.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.question: Polypharmacy is most commonly defined as the concurrent use of how many regular medicines?
options: Two or more regular medicines
Three or more regular medicines
Ten or more regular medicines
Five or more regular medicines
Any medicine continued beyond twelve months
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.explanation: Polypharmacy is commonly defined as ≥5 regular medicines. The clinically important issue, however, is PROBLEMATIC (inappropriate) polypharmacy, not simply the number of drugs.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.question: What does the STOPP part of the STOPP/START criteria identify?
options: Potentially Inappropriate Medications (PIMs) that should be considered for stopping
Beneficial drugs that are missing and should be started
The correct doses for renal impairment
Drugs that require therapeutic monitoring
Over-the-counter medicines only
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.answer: Potentially Inappropriate Medications (PIMs) that should be considered for stopping
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.explanation: STOPP (Screening Tool of Older Persons' Prescriptions) flags Potentially Inappropriate Medications - drugs to consider STOPPING. START, by contrast, flags Potential Prescribing Omissions - beneficial drugs that should be started.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.question: Which principle is central to the STOPP/START approach?
options: Only over-prescribing counts as a prescribing error
Prescribing omissions are handled separately from review
Inappropriate prescribing is bidirectional — both directions
Deprescribing means stopping every non-essential drug
The total drug count is the main determinant of harm
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.answer: Inappropriate prescribing is bidirectional — both directions
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.explanation: STOPP/START captures that inappropriate prescribing is BIDIRECTIONAL: under-prescribing (e.g. no anticoagulation in AF, no statin post-MI, no bone protection after fragility fracture) is as much an error as over-prescribing. Optimisation - not blind cutting - is the aim.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.question: An 84-year-old with atrial fibrillation and a high stroke risk is on no anticoagulant and has no contraindication. This is an example of which prescribing problem, addressed by which tool?
options: Over-prescribing; STOPP
Appropriate polypharmacy; no action
A prescribing cascade; STOPPFrail
Duplication; Beers criteria
Under-prescribing (a prescribing omission); START
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.explanation: Missing anticoagulation in AF (where indicated and safe) is a Potential Prescribing OMISSION - under-prescribing - which the START criteria flag for initiation. It is an error just as much as over-prescribing.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.question: A frail 88-year-old on a benzodiazepine for years has had recurrent falls and daytime drowsiness. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Continue it unchanged, as she is long accustomed to it
Reduce the dose in stages and stop, monitoring for withdrawal
Add a stimulant during the day to offset the drowsiness
Double the dose to improve her night-time sleep quality
Switch her to a longer-acting benzodiazepine instead
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.answer: Reduce the dose in stages and stop, monitoring for withdrawal
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.explanation: A long-term benzodiazepine in a frail older person with recurrent falls and daytime drowsiness is a classic STOPP target. It should be reduced in stages and stopped rather than continued or substituted, monitoring for withdrawal — abrupt cessation risks a withdrawal syndrome including seizures.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.question: A patient develops ankle oedema after starting amlodipine, and a diuretic is added to treat it. What does this illustrate?
options: Appropriate polypharmacy
A drug allergy
Under-prescribing
A prescribing cascade
A pharmacokinetic interaction
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.explanation: Treating a drug's side-effect (amlodipine-induced ankle oedema) with another drug (a diuretic), rather than recognising and addressing the cause, is a PRESCRIBING CASCADE - a driver of problematic polypharmacy.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.question: Which of the following is a common START recommendation (a beneficial drug that is often omitted)?
options: Bone protection (bisphosphonate + calcium/vitamin D) after a fragility fracture
A long-term full-dose PPI with no indication
An anticholinergic for urinary frequency in a faller
An NSAID in a patient with CKD
A duplicate drug from the same class
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.answer: Bone protection (bisphosphonate + calcium/vitamin D) after a fragility fracture
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.explanation: START flags beneficial omissions such as bone protection after a fragility fracture, anticoagulation in AF, and statin/ACE inhibitor/antiplatelet in cardiovascular disease. The other options are STOPP targets (drugs to reconsider/stop).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.question: An 82-year-old with chronic kidney disease and atrial fibrillation on apixaban asks for something for her knee pain. Which prescription would a STOPP review flag?
options: Paracetamol taken regularly alongside a proton pump inhibitor
An inhaled corticosteroid with a spacer in stable asthma
An NSAID in a patient with chronic kidney disease
A statin for secondary prevention after myocardial infarction
Calcium with vitamin D in a housebound care-home resident
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.answer: An NSAID in a patient with chronic kidney disease
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.explanation: NSAIDs in patients with CKD, heart failure, or on anticoagulants are a STOPP target due to the risk of GI bleeding and acute kidney injury. The other options are appropriate or beneficial.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.question: Why are older people more susceptible to drug accumulation and toxicity?
options: Increased renal clearance, so drugs are eliminated faster
Faster hepatic first-pass metabolism, lowering blood levels
Lower body fat, which shortens the half-life of lipophilic drugs
Reduced pharmacodynamic sensitivity to CNS depressant drugs
Reduced renal clearance and increased sensitivity, amplified by frailty
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.answer: Reduced renal clearance and increased sensitivity, amplified by frailty
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.explanation: Ageing brings REDUCED renal clearance (drug accumulation), reduced albumin (more free drug), altered body composition (longer half-life of lipophilic drugs), and INCREASED pharmacodynamic sensitivity - all amplified by the frailty 'multiplier', so small drug effects cause big harm.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.question: What does the Anticholinergic Burden (ACB) score quantify, and why does it matter?
options: The renal excretion of each drug in the regimen
Cumulative anticholinergic load across the whole regimen
The total number of regular drugs a patient takes
The QTc-prolonging effect of the whole regimen combined
The monthly prescribing cost of the medication list
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.answer: Cumulative anticholinergic load across the whole regimen
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.explanation: The ACB score sums the anticholinergic load of every drug in the regimen, including ones not thought of as anticholinergic. A total of 3 or more is the high-burden threshold, associated with delirium, cognitive decline, falls and mortality, making it a key target for medication review — reducing agents such as oxybutynin, tricyclics and sedating antihistamines.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.question: An older patient with advanced frailty and a life expectancy of a few months is taking a statin and a bisphosphonate. Which tool and action are most appropriate?
options: START criteria; add further preventive treatment
Beers criteria; continue the statin but stop the bisphosphonate
Continue both indefinitely, whatever the prognosis
STOPPFrail; consider deprescribing preventive drugs
Anticholinergic burden score; the burden is unaffected
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.explanation: STOPPFrail provides deprescribing criteria for frail older people with limited life expectancy. Preventive drugs like statins and bisphosphonates, whose benefit is only long-term, can be stopped to prioritise symptom control and quality of life.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.question: What is the correct FIRST step of a structured medication (7-Steps) review?
options: Establish what matters to the patient
Stop the most expensive drug on the list
Check serum levels of every drug the patient takes
Halve the dose of every regular medicine
Refer to a specialist before making any change
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.answer: Establish what matters to the patient
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.explanation: The 7-Steps review begins with the AIM - understanding what matters to the patient (their goals, life expectancy and values) - before identifying essential drugs, unnecessary drugs, whether goals are met, safety issues, cost-effectiveness, and whether the patient is willing/able.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.question: Which drugs typically need to be TAPERED rather than stopped abruptly during deprescribing?
options: Paracetamol and calcium supplements
Amlodipine and other calcium-channel blockers
Benzodiazepines, opioids, corticosteroids and beta-blockers
Levothyroxine and other hormone replacement
Inhaled salbutamol used as required
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.explanation: Benzodiazepines, opioids, corticosteroids, beta-blockers and some antidepressants must be TAPERED, to avoid a withdrawal syndrome, rebound angina or hypertension, and adrenal insufficiency. Deprescribing should be a shared decision, prioritising the drug of greatest harm and least benefit, ideally one change at a time, with monitoring for withdrawal or return of the condition.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.question: A 79-year-old with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction takes an ACE inhibitor, a beta-blocker and a loop diuretic. She is well, her symptoms are controlled and her renal function is stable. How should her regimen be viewed at medication review?
options: Problematic polypharmacy that requires urgent deprescribing
A prescribing cascade, since each drug treats the last one's effect
An anticholinergic burden problem needing a burden score
An automatic STOPP violation because of the drug count
Appropriate polypharmacy — continue and monitor
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polyphar.explanation: Several drugs, each with a valid current indication and net benefit, is APPROPRIATE polypharmacy - it should be continued and monitored, not cut. Problematic polypharmacy refers to unnecessary, harmful or duplicated drugs whose harms outweigh benefits.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.question: What is the fundamental mechanism of a pressure ulcer?
options: Bacterial invasion through intact, healthy skin
An autoimmune attack directed against the dermis
Arterial embolism to the cutaneous circulation
Sustained pressure occluding capillaries, causing necrosis
Type IV allergic contact dermatitis from the mattress
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.answer: Sustained pressure occluding capillaries, causing necrosis
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.explanation: A pressure ulcer results from sustained pressure (+/- shear) over a bony prominence that occludes capillaries, producing local ischaemia, hypoxia and tissue necrosis. It is not primarily infective, autoimmune, embolic or allergic.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.question: Which is the single most important risk factor for developing a pressure ulcer?
options: Immobility
Hypertension
Male sex
Raised serum cholesterol
Mild hypothyroidism
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.explanation: Immobility (bed- or chair-bound, sedation, paralysis, post-operative, a long lie) is the biggest single risk factor. Anaemia, extremes of BMI, malnutrition, incontinence and moisture, poor perfusion, reduced sensation and frailty all contribute, but immobility is dominant.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.question: An immobile elderly inpatient has an area of non-blanchable redness over the sacrum, with intact skin. What category of pressure ulcer is this, and what is the priority?
options: Category 3; arrange surgical debridement
Category 4; refer urgently to plastic surgery
Category 1; offload and intensify SSKIN prevention
Unstageable; leave it alone until it is debrided
Deep tissue injury; start systemic antibiotics
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.answer: Category 1; offload and intensify SSKIN prevention
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.explanation: Non-blanchable erythema of INTACT skin is a Category 1 pressure ulcer. The priority is to offload the pressure immediately and intensify prevention (the SSKIN bundle) to prevent progression. Debridement/antibiotics are not indicated at this stage.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.question: A pressure ulcer shows full-thickness tissue loss with visible bone and tendon at its base. What category is this?
options: Category 1
Category 2
Category 3
Unstageable
Category 4
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.explanation: Exposed bone, tendon or muscle indicates a Category 4 pressure ulcer (full-thickness tissue loss). Category 3 shows visible subcutaneous fat but NOT exposed bone/muscle; Category 2 is partial-thickness (dermis).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.question: A sacral pressure ulcer has full-thickness loss but its base is completely covered by thick brown eschar, so depth cannot be seen. How is this categorised?
options: Category 2
Unstageable
Category 3
Category 4
Deep tissue injury
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.explanation: When the wound base is obscured by slough/eschar so depth cannot be determined, it is UNSTAGEABLE - the true depth can only be categorised once debrided (Category 3 or 4).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.question: Which set of measures forms the SSKIN pressure-ulcer prevention bundle?
options: Steroids, Saline, Kaolin, Iodine, NSAIDs
Surface, Swabbing, Keep moving, Infection control, Nutrition
Support surface, Skin inspection, Kilocalories, Incontinence, NSAIDs
Surface, Skin inspection, Keep moving, Incontinence, Nutrition
Screening, Statins, Ketones, Insulin, Nebulisers
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.answer: Surface, Skin inspection, Keep moving, Incontinence, Nutrition
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.explanation: SSKIN = Surface (pressure-redistributing mattress/cushion), Skin inspection, Keep moving (reposition), Incontinence/moisture management, and Nutrition/hydration. It is the core prevention framework.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.question: How frequently should a HIGH-RISK patient be repositioned to prevent pressure ulcers?
options: At least every 4 hours
At least every 6 hours
At least every 2 hours, whatever the support surface
At least every 12 hours
Only when the patient reports discomfort
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.explanation: High-risk adults are repositioned at least every 4 hours; adults assessed as at risk, at least every 6 hours — more often if the skin changes or the person is uncomfortable. The schedule is documented and heels are offloaded. Two-hourly turning is traditional teaching rather than the stated minimum.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.question: A healthcare assistant asks whether rubbing a reddened but intact area over a patient's sacrum would help prevent it breaking down. What is the correct advice?
options: Encourage it, as massage prevents ulcers
Massage only with oil
Do NOT massage or rub skin over bony prominences, as it causes damage
Massage for at least 10 minutes
Apply heat as well
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.answer: Do NOT massage or rub skin over bony prominences, as it causes damage
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.explanation: NICE advises AGAINST skin massage/rubbing over bony prominences to prevent pressure ulcers - it causes tissue damage. Prevention is via offloading, repositioning, surfaces, skin care and nutrition (SSKIN).

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.question: What is the FIRST priority in managing an established pressure ulcer?
options: Start broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics
Take a superficial wound swab for culture
Pack the wound with dry gauze and review
Refer immediately for reconstructive skin grafting
Offload the pressure immediately
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.explanation: Nothing heals under continued pressure, so the first priority is to OFFLOAD (reposition + appropriate support surface), then categorise/document and dress the wound. Antibiotics, routine swabs and grafting are not the first step.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.question: A pressure ulcer looks clean and is healing, with no spreading erythema, systemic upset or increased pain. Should a wound swab and antibiotics be given?
options: Yes — swab and treat every pressure ulcer routinely
No — swab and treat only if clinically infected
Yes — give a prophylactic oral antibiotic course
Yes — but use a topical antibiotic rather than oral
No — but send a swab anyway so the result is on file
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.answer: No — swab and treat only if clinically infected
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.explanation: All open pressure ulcers are colonised, so a swab from a clean, healing ulcer will grow organisms that do not need treating. Swab and give systemic antibiotics only with clinical signs of infection — spreading erythema, heat, increasing pain, systemic upset or delayed healing — and take any sample from the cleansed wound bed rather than the surface. Topical antibiotics are not used at all, because of sensitisation and resistance.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.question: A stable, dry, black eschar is present over a heel pressure ulcer, with no signs of infection or instability. What is the appropriate management?
options: Sharp debride the eschar on the ward the same day
Apply a moist gauze pack to soften and lift it
Start intravenous antibiotics and review in 48 hours
Leave the stable dry eschar intact and offload the heel
Refer urgently for below-knee amputation
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.answer: Leave the stable dry eschar intact and offload the heel
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.explanation: A stable, dry heel eschar is often LEFT INTACT as it acts as a protective cover, unless there are signs of infection or instability. The heel should be offloaded. Debridement is reserved for slough/necrosis where healing is the goal and the eschar is unstable/infected.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.question: In a patient with darkly pigmented skin, how is early pressure damage best detected?
options: Purplish discolouration plus temperature, firmness and pain changes
Bright red erythema is the only reliable early sign
By waiting until an open wound has formed to categorise
By sending a wound swab for culture and sensitivities
Early damage cannot be detected in darkly pigmented skin
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.answer: Purplish discolouration plus temperature, firmness and pain changes
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.explanation: In darker skin tones, early damage may not appear as redness; look for purplish/bluish discolouration and changes in temperature, firmness or the patient reporting pain, and PALPATE rather than relying on visual redness alone.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.question: A frail nursing-home resident is admitted with a large, deep sacral pressure ulcer, alongside dehydration, poor hygiene and no record of any repositioning or risk assessment. Besides wound management, what should be considered?
options: Wound care alone, with no further escalation
Discharge straight back to the nursing home
An adult-safeguarding referral
A capacity assessment before any wound care is given
Withholding dressings until the ulcer has been swabbed
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.explanation: Pressure damage of this severity alongside dehydration, poor hygiene and no record of repositioning or risk assessment suggests omissions in care, so an adult-safeguarding referral should be considered and the ulcer reported as a patient-safety incident. All pressure ulcers are recorded and reviewed for learning — the older avoidable/unavoidable labelling is no longer used.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.question: What is the appropriate dressing approach for most pressure ulcers?
options: Dry gauze changed several times a day
Leaving the wound open to the air to dry out
Daily antiseptic soaks and nothing else
Occlusive tape applied directly over the wound bed
Moisture-retaining dressings matched to exudate
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.explanation: Pressure ulcers are dressed to maintain a MOIST wound environment (hydrocolloids, foams, alginates, hydrogels) matched to the exudate level. Routine dry gauze is avoided as it is adherent and painful.

conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.question: Which serious complication can arise from a long-standing, chronic non-healing pressure ulcer?
options: Basal cell carcinoma arising at the wound edge
Marjolin's ulcer (squamous cell carcinoma)
Malignant melanoma developing within the scar
Kaposi's sarcoma in the granulation tissue
A benign lipoma beneath the wound bed
conditions__GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure.explanation: A chronic non-healing wound (including a long-standing pressure ulcer) can rarely undergo malignant change to a squamous cell carcinoma - a Marjolin's ulcer. Other serious complications include cellulitis, osteomyelitis and sepsis.
